meta.blurb: Dev says his lucky socks help his team win. His friend Ines asks how they could know. At the school Question Club, they learn to test ideas fairly, spot how we fool ourselves and say I might be wrong.
meta.bible:
Ines: a twelve-year-old girl who always asks how do we know. Dev: her best friend, cheerful, a goalkeeper in the school football team, owner of lucky socks. Ms Rao: their science teacher, patient and funny, who runs the Question Club on Thursdays. Mr Bello: a neighbour who believes in a magnetic wristband. The story takes place in one school term at a school with a science room and a football field. Key terms: Hypothesis, Hypotheses, Variable, Variables, Control, Experiment, Experiments, Observation, Prediction, Evidence, Placebo, Blind, Bias, Confirmation, Anecdote, Anecdotes, Correlation, Cause, Sample, Replication, Peer, Review, Falsifiable, Theory, Uncertainty, Statistics, Survivorship, Pseudoscience, Pareidolia, Occam, Razor, Scurvy, Consensus, Cherry. Real history, told accurately: James Lind tested treatments for scurvy on twelve sailors in 1747; Ignaz Semmelweis in Vienna in 1847 asked doctors to wash their hands with a chlorine solution and deaths fell; Louis Pasteur used flasks with long curved necks in the 1860s; Eratosthenes estimated the size of the Earth about 240 BC with shadows in Syene and Alexandria; Arthur Eddington and others measured the bending of starlight during the eclipse of 1919; Abraham Wald studied where returning bombers were hit in the Second World War. In 2015 a large team repeated 100 psychology experiments and fewer than half gave the same clear result. Voice: friendly, curious, never superior; examples are true or clearly made up for the story; no real living people named. Added for the full-length book: Amara: a quiet club member who draws charts and counts carefully. Tomas: a cheerful, talkative club member who guesses quickly and learns to check. Coach Hall: the football coach, who films matches and keeps the results sheet. Mr Bello is a retired bus driver who grows tomatoes. Priya and Joel: two older pupils who join the club later. Kofi: Ines's seven-year-old brother. Mr Silva: a teacher friend of Ms Rao in a town about 300 kilometres to the north. The story runs from September to December in one school term.
 More key terms: Storks, Wristband, Blindfolded, Survivorship, Armour, Bomber, Bombers, Lemons, Oranges, Cider, Vinegar, Sailors, Salisbury, Pfungst, Oskar, Clever, Hans, Franklin, Benjamin, Wald, Abraham.
 More real history, told accurately: Jakob Kolletschka, a friend of Semmelweis, died in 1847 after a scalpel cut; Joseph Lister used clean surgery in the 1860s; Francesco Redi tested meat in jars in 1668; Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw tiny living things through his lenses in the 1670s; Felix Pouchet argued against Pasteur. Key terms: Maggots, Hungarian, Italian, Dutch, Vienna, Lister, Joseph, Jakob, Kolletschka, Redi, Francesco, Leeuwenhoek, Antonie, Pouchet, Felix, Mould.
 More real history, told accurately: Eratosthenes, a Greek librarian in Alexandria, about 240 BC; Syene and Alexandria; a stadion was a Greek unit of length of uncertain size; the Earth is about 40,000 kilometres around. In 1919 Arthur Eddington and others photographed stars near the Sun at a total eclipse on 29 May, at Principe and at Sobral in Brazil, to test Albert Einstein's theory against Isaac Newton's. Key terms: Principe, Sobral, Brazil, Isaac, Newton, Albert, Einstein, Eratosthenes, Egypt, Greek, Greeks, Stadia, Stadion, Alexandria, Syene, London, Africa, America, Moon.
 More real history, told accurately: black swans were seen in Western Australia by the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh in 1697; Alfred Wegener suggested drifting continents in 1912 and most experts accepted plate tectonics only in the 1960s; the common cold is caused by viruses, not by cold air. Key terms: Willem, Vlamingh, Dutch, Australia, Western, Alfred, Wegener, German, Sparkle, Tonic, Viruses, Falsifiable, Pseudoscience, Dowsing.
chapters: Measuring the Earth With a Stick

beats.scene: Dev pulls on a pair of striped lucky socks beside a football goal
beats.summary: Dev says his lucky socks help his team win, and Ines asks how they could know.

beats.scene: A crumpled list of football wins lies open on a school desk
beats.summary: Dev shows Ines his list of won matches, each marked with the words striped socks.

beats.scene: Dev raises both gloves in the goal while his teammates cheer
beats.summary: Dev's team wins another match, and he is sure it was the socks.

beats.scene: A bright poster on the school noticeboard reads Question Club, Thursdays
beats.summary: Ines and Dev see Ms Rao's poster inviting anyone curious to a new Question Club.

beats.scene: Mr Bello waves over his garden fence, a shiny band on his wrist
beats.summary: On the way home they pass Mr Bello, a friendly neighbour who wears a magnetic wristband.

beats.scene: Four children sit in the science room while Ms Rao writes on the whiteboard
beats.summary: On Thursday Ines, Dev, Amara and Tomas arrive for the first meeting of the Question Club.

beats.scene: Ms Rao holds a thick textbook above her head in front of the class
beats.summary: Ms Rao says science is a way of finding out, not a pile of facts.

beats.scene: Two rules are written in blue marker beneath the name of the club
beats.summary: The club's two rules are to ask how we know and to be ready to say I might be wrong.

beats.scene: Ms Rao shakes a sealed shoebox while the children lean close to listen
beats.summary: Ms Rao gives the club a sealed box and asks them to work out what is inside without opening it.

beats.scene: Ms Rao lifts the shoebox lid to show a toy car and a pencil
beats.summary: The box opens to show a toy car and a pencil, and Ms Rao says a careful guess is a fine beginning.

beats.scene: Four children bend over open notebooks as Ms Rao points to a page
beats.summary: Ms Rao shows the club how to keep a notebook with the date, place, weather and plain observations.

beats.scene: Ines holds a magnifying glass over a leaf with tiny holes in it
beats.summary: Science starts with careful observation: looking closely, noticing and recording.

beats.scene: A notebook page is divided into two columns by a line down the middle
beats.summary: Ms Rao shows the difference between what we see and what we think about it.

beats.scene: Tomas points at the leaf while Ms Rao raises one eyebrow
beats.summary: Tomas insists that bugs made the holes, and Ms Rao asks what he actually saw.

beats.scene: The club walks across the school field with notebooks, past puddles and a hedge
beats.summary: The club walks around the school field and writes down everything they notice.

beats.scene: Amara kneels beside a line of ants with a stopwatch in her hand
beats.summary: Amara counts how many ants pass one point in a minute, using a stopwatch.

beats.scene: Three bowls of water, cold, warm and hot, stand in a row
beats.summary: A three-bowl test shows that our senses can be fooled and that instruments are more reliable.

beats.scene: Two straight lines with arrowheads pointing in and out, and a ruler beside them
beats.summary: An optical illusion shows two lines that look different but measure the same.

beats.scene: Dev draws the match from memory while Ines checks a video on her phone
beats.summary: Dev tries to remember a recent match and finds that his memory has changed the details.

beats.scene: Ines's notebook page lists five numbered questions in tidy handwriting
beats.summary: Ines ends the day with five new questions that her observations raised.

beats.scene: Dev raises his hand and asks a question while the club members look puzzled
beats.summary: A good question is one that can be tested and answered with evidence.

beats.scene: Six questions on the board, some ticked and some crossed out
beats.summary: Ms Rao lists questions on the board and the club sorts those that science can answer from those it cannot.

beats.scene: Tomas holds a speaker beside a pot plant as Ms Rao watches
beats.summary: Tomas asks whether plants grow better with music, and Ms Rao asks him how he would measure better.

beats.scene: Ines draws a list of three suspects: a caterpillar, a snail and the wind
beats.summary: Ines lists several possible explanations for the holes in the leaf.

beats.scene: Ines writes a guess on a card and pins it next to the leaf
beats.summary: A hypothesis is a testable guess about an explanation; it must be able to be wrong.

beats.scene: Ines lists what she expects to see if the caterpillar guess is true
beats.summary: A prediction says what we should see if the hypothesis is true.

beats.scene: Ines spots a small green caterpillar on the underside of a leaf
beats.summary: Ines goes outside and finds a caterpillar and droppings, which fits her prediction.

beats.scene: Tomas raises a hand while Ms Rao shakes her head with a smile
beats.summary: Ms Rao says the evidence supports the idea but does not prove it, since other creatures may also have visited.

beats.scene: Dev writes on a fresh card while Ines watches over his shoulder
beats.summary: Dev writes his lucky socks idea as a hypothesis that could be shown to be wrong.

beats.scene: Dev and Ines pause in the doorway, looking back at the card
beats.summary: Dev admits he is nervous that the test may show the socks do nothing, but he agrees to a fair test.

beats.scene: Ms Rao pours dried beans from a paper bag into a bowl of water
beats.summary: Ms Rao shows how to start a bean test: soak the seeds and choose matching ones.

beats.scene: Tomas sets a big pot of rich soil beside a small pot of sand
beats.summary: Tomas sets up a test in which many things differ, and the club spots why it is unfair.

beats.scene: Two matching pots of beans stand by a sunny window and a dark cupboard
beats.summary: A fair test changes one thing at a time and keeps everything else the same.

beats.scene: A chart on the wall lists words: change, measure, keep the same, compare
beats.summary: The thing you change, the thing you measure and the things you keep the same are variables; a control is a comparison.

beats.scene: Amara writes labels on pots and plants three beans in each one
beats.summary: They plant three beans in each pot so that one unlucky seed cannot spoil the test.

beats.scene: Ines measures a bean shoot with a ruler while Dev writes the number down
beats.summary: Measure with numbers and units instead of guessing: use a ruler, a clock or a scale.

beats.scene: A table of daily bean heights lies beside a pencil line graph
beats.summary: Amara turns the daily numbers into a graph that shows how each pot is growing.

beats.scene: The caretaker waters a pot from a small jug while the club watches
beats.summary: The caretaker waters one pot by mistake, and the club records the slip instead of hiding it.

beats.scene: Pale, tall bean shoots lean in the cupboard beside short green ones
beats.summary: The bean plants in the dark grow tall, thin and pale, which surprises everyone.

beats.scene: Ines writes her prediction and the real result side by side in her notebook
beats.summary: Ines predicted that the sunny beans would be tallest, was wrong, and learns that a surprise is useful.

beats.scene: A hand tosses a coin above a table covered with small tally marks
beats.summary: A few trials can mislead, but many trials show the pattern; a bigger sample is more reliable.

beats.scene: Four children toss coins and make tally marks on a shared sheet
beats.summary: Each child tosses a fair coin ten times, and the numbers of heads all differ.

beats.scene: Ms Rao adds long columns of tally marks on the board in two colours
beats.summary: Combining the tosses of a whole class gives 104 heads in 200, close to half, so a pattern appears.

beats.scene: Amara holds a clipboard and asks a crowd of pupils about school lunch
beats.summary: A sample should be big enough and fair, so asking 50 pupils tells more than asking two friends.

beats.scene: Coloured dice lie scattered on a table beside a wobbly graph
beats.summary: Rolling a die 60 times gives each number about ten times, but not exactly, so the graph wobbles.

beats.scene: Several coloured dice lie scattered on a table beside a graph with wobbly lines
beats.summary: Chance causes results to vary, so scientists look at averages and repeated results.

beats.scene: Ines and Amara measure the same bean shoot with two different rulers
beats.summary: Two people measure the same shoot and get slightly different numbers, because every measurement has a small error.

beats.scene: Amara writes three measurements and their average on the whiteboard
beats.summary: Averaging several measurements gives a steadier number than any single one.

beats.scene: Dev dives for a ball in goal, with three ticks drawn above him
beats.summary: A run of three saves can happen by chance, so one lucky streak proves little.

beats.scene: Two long rows of H and T letters are written on the board
beats.summary: People who write a fake random row leave out long streaks, so Ms Rao spots the row from a real coin.

beats.scene: The beans on two windowsills are measured again by two new club members
beats.summary: Replication: other people repeating an experiment and getting the same result makes it stronger.

beats.scene: Priya and Joel measure bean shoots in another classroom beside a table of numbers
beats.summary: The two new pupils, Priya and Joel, get slightly different numbers but the same pattern, and they join the club.

beats.scene: Scientists in two different laboratories compare the same results on matching charts
beats.summary: Scientists ask other laboratories to repeat important experiments before they trust them.

beats.scene: Priya follows Ines's written steps and stops at the words some water
beats.summary: Ines writes the method as exact steps so that another person can repeat it, and learns to be precise.

beats.scene: Coach Hall and the club plan the sock test on a clipboard
beats.summary: Coach Hall agrees to help, and the club plans 40 penalty kicks, 20 in each pair of socks.

beats.scene: A whiteboard lists the rules: what counts as a save, who kicks, how many
beats.summary: The club decides the rules before the test, including what counts as a save.

beats.scene: Slips of folded paper lie inside a hat beside two pairs of socks
beats.summary: Slips in a hat decide which socks Dev wears for each block of five kicks, so that chance sets the order.

beats.scene: Dev crouches in goal on the cold field as Amara prepares to kick
beats.summary: On a cold Saturday morning Dev faces 40 kicks while Ines records every result.

beats.scene: A results table shows striped socks eight saves and plain socks seven
beats.summary: Dev saved 8 of 20 in the lucky socks and 7 of 20 in the plain socks, a gap that chance could easily explain.

beats.scene: Dev sits on the damp grass holding the striped socks in both hands
beats.summary: Dev is disappointed but admits the test was fair, because a result is a result.

beats.scene: Dev sits on a bench with his striped socks beside him, thinking hard
beats.summary: Dev says the socks still feel lucky, and Ms Rao says a feeling is real but is not evidence.

beats.scene: Ines looks up at a cloud shaped like a face and laughs
beats.summary: Our brains see patterns, even in clouds and random dots.

beats.scene: A sheet of random dots has a loop drawn around one cluster
beats.summary: Random dots form clusters that look like shapes, showing that real chance is lumpy.

beats.scene: A blurry view of a Martian hill with shadows like eyes
beats.summary: A 1976 spacecraft photograph of a hill on Mars looked like a face, but sharper pictures showed an ordinary hill.

beats.scene: The numbers two, four and six on the board beside a question mark
beats.summary: Ms Rao's number game shows that we test a guess by seeking examples that fit it, not ones that might break it.

beats.scene: Dev counts tally marks on a page of green ticks and few red crosses
beats.summary: Confirmation bias: we notice what supports our beliefs and forget what does not.

beats.scene: Tomas holds a ringing phone while a thought bubble shows his cousin
beats.summary: We count the times a coincidence happens and forget the many times nothing happens.

beats.scene: Pupils read identical slips of paper with looks of surprise
beats.summary: Every pupil thinks a description fits them, though all received the same text, which shows how vague words fit anyone.

beats.scene: Ines writes three numbered rules on a page, with a pencil behind her ear
beats.summary: The club lists ways to avoid fooling ourselves: write the prediction first, count the misses, and ask someone else to check.

beats.scene: Ines walks home alone beneath a sky of scattered clouds
beats.summary: Ines realises that the easiest person to fool is yourself.

beats.scene: Mr Bello holds up a metal wristband over the garden fence
beats.summary: A single story, an anecdote, is not good evidence; many cases tested fairly are.

beats.scene: Ines and Dev at the fence as Mr Bello offers tomatoes
beats.summary: Ines asks Mr Bello when his back improved, and he says it was about three weeks after he bought the band.

beats.scene: Ines writes a list of changes: rest, a new chair, warm weather
beats.summary: Ines lists everything else that changed in those three weeks, any of which could have helped his back.

beats.scene: A wobbly line graph of pain rises to a peak and then slowly falls
beats.summary: People try a remedy when their pain is at its worst, and pain often eases by itself afterwards.

beats.scene: A crowd at a bus stop, only one person raising a hand
beats.summary: People who felt no change from the wristband rarely tell their stories, so we hear only the successes.

beats.scene: Amara pins magazine adverts with happy faces onto a corkboard
beats.summary: Amara collects adverts full of happy customer quotes, and the club notes that none of them can be checked.

beats.scene: Tomas tells his story beside a poster of a car seat belt
beats.summary: Tomas says his uncle never wore a seat belt and lived to 90, but studies of many crashes show that seat belts save lives.

beats.scene: Ines sketches two groups of stick figures, one wearing bands and one not
beats.summary: Ines sketches a first design for a fair test of the wristband, and Ms Rao asks what might still be wrong with it.

beats.scene: Mr Bello hands Ines a paper bag of tomatoes over the fence
beats.summary: Ines does not want to hurt Mr Bello's feelings, and Ms Rao says that kindness and curiosity go together.

beats.scene: Ines writes a note at the top of an empty notebook page
beats.summary: Ines decides to wait until she knows how to design a proper test, and then to ask Mr Bello kindly.

beats.scene: Ines holds two identical white pills in her open palm
beats.summary: The placebo effect: people can feel better just because they expect a treatment to work.

beats.scene: A calm hospital room with a sugar pill on a white saucer
beats.summary: Expectation can change how we feel, mostly pain and tiredness, but it cannot mend a broken bone.

beats.scene: Two cups of the same juice, one with a fancy label
beats.summary: The same juice tastes better with a fancy label, which shows how expectation changes experience.

beats.scene: Ines draws two circles labelled treatment group and dummy group
beats.summary: A good medicine test compares a group that gets the treatment with a group that gets a dummy.

beats.scene: Two groups of volunteers receive plain envelopes from a researcher in a white coat
beats.summary: In blind tests, people do not know which treatment they get; in double-blind tests, nor do the researchers.

beats.scene: A horse taps a hoof on cobblestones while a crowd watches in a courtyard
beats.summary: A horse called Clever Hans seemed to do sums, but he was reading tiny signals from the people around him.

beats.scene: Men in old-fashioned coats blindfold a woman beside a tree in a garden
beats.summary: In 1784 a French committee that included Benjamin Franklin blindfolded patients to test a healer's magnetic claim.

beats.scene: Numbered cups stand in a row while Tomas sips with his eyes shut
beats.summary: Tomas tries to tell tap water from bottled water blind and gets about half right, as chance predicts.

beats.scene: Names written on paper slips are drawn from a cloth bag
beats.summary: Choosing groups by lot, not by choice, spreads hidden differences evenly between the groups.

beats.scene: Ines draws a plan: matching bands, a coded list, a pain scale
beats.summary: Ines redraws her wristband test with identical bands, random groups, nobody knowing who wears which, and a daily pain score.

beats.scene: A weary sailor leans on the rail of a ship at sea
beats.summary: Scurvy made sailors weak and sick on long voyages and killed huge numbers of them.

beats.scene: A ship's doctor holds up bottles of vinegar and cider
beats.summary: Many cures were proposed, from fresh air to vinegar, and each had happy stories but no fair test.

beats.scene: James Lind writes by candlelight in a cramped cabin on a wooden warship
beats.summary: In 1747 the naval surgeon James Lind decided to test the cures on a ship at sea.

beats.scene: Twelve sick sailors sit on hammocks in a lamplit part of the ship
beats.summary: Lind chose twelve sailors whose cases were as alike as he could find, on the same diet.

beats.scene: Six pairs of sailors each hold a different cup or bottle
beats.summary: Lind divided the men into six pairs and gave each pair a different treatment.

beats.scene: Dev points from the bean chart to a list of six pairs
beats.summary: The club sees that Lind changed one thing, the treatment, and kept the rest the same, as with the bean pots.

beats.scene: Two sailors eat oranges and a lemon while others lie weak in hammocks
beats.summary: After about six days the pair given oranges and a lemon were far better, and one was fit for duty.

beats.scene: A tiny table of results sits beside a question mark about sample size
beats.summary: Ms Rao says Lind's test was small, with twelve men, but its careful design made it convincing.

beats.scene: Barrels of lemons are loaded onto a navy ship in a busy harbour
beats.summary: Lind published in 1753, the navy took decades to act, and the cause, a lack of vitamin C, was found much later.

beats.scene: Dev peels an orange as he and Ines walk home along a lane
beats.summary: Dev says twelve sailors did more good than a thousand opinions, and Ines wonders what to do when a fair test is not possible.

beats.scene: A graph shows two lines rising together, labelled ice cream and swimming
beats.summary: Correlation is not cause: two things can rise together without one causing the other.

beats.scene: A chart matches bigger shoe sizes with higher reading scores
beats.summary: Children with bigger feet read better, but age explains both.

beats.scene: A detective's board shows many arrows and question marks tied by red string
beats.summary: A confounder is a hidden third factor; scientists try to rule these out.

beats.scene: Two arrows between a team captain and a goal count point in both directions
beats.summary: Sometimes cause and effect run the other way round: good players become captains, not the reverse.

beats.scene: A stork stands on a chimney above the roofs of a village
beats.summary: Across European countries, those with more storks have more babies, but bigger countries simply have more of both.

beats.scene: Two jagged lines on a chart match perfectly beneath silly titles
beats.summary: If you compare thousands of pairs of numbers, some pairs will match by pure chance.

beats.scene: Lind's pairs, bean pots and name slips are arranged together on a table
beats.summary: Experiments that assign groups by chance spread hidden factors evenly, so a difference is more likely to come from the treatment.

beats.scene: Doctors in the 1950s fill in questionnaires beside tall stacks of paper files
beats.summary: When an experiment is impossible, as with smoking, scientists follow thousands of people over many years instead.

beats.scene: Five arrows from five different studies all point the same way
beats.summary: Evidence about cause is strongest when many studies agree, the cause comes first, and there is a believable reason.

beats.scene: Ines pins a card on the wall that reads Linked is not caused
beats.summary: The club writes a rule on the wall: when two things are linked, ask what else might link them.

beats.scene: Ms Rao draws a bomber on the board and dots it with red marker
beats.summary: Ms Rao sets a puzzle: returning planes are covered in bullet holes, so where should the armour go?

beats.scene: Tomas draws armour over the red dots while Amara frowns
beats.summary: Tomas says to armour the places with holes, and Ms Rao asks which planes the club is looking at.

beats.scene: Abraham Wald writes sums at a desk piled with paper
beats.summary: The mathematician Abraham Wald saw that the holes showed where a plane could be hit and still fly home.

beats.scene: Red dots avoid the engine on the drawing, which is circled in blue
beats.summary: So the armour should go where the returning planes had no holes, such as around the engines.

beats.scene: Pages of calculations fill a desk beneath a green lamp
beats.summary: The tidy story is simplified: Wald actually did long calculations to estimate how likely a plane was to survive a hit.

beats.scene: A lone tree stands on a hill where a forest was cut down
beats.summary: Drawing conclusions only from the survivors is called survivorship bias.

beats.scene: A street of old stone houses stands beside a modern glass building
beats.summary: Old buildings seem beautiful and well built because the ugly and weak ones were pulled down long ago.

beats.scene: Dev holds a clipboard and questions players in football shirts
beats.summary: Dev asks the team whether football is fun, but the players who quit are not there to ask.

beats.scene: A glossy magazine cover shows a smiling person beside a yacht
beats.summary: Stories of famous people who succeeded after quitting school hide the thousands who quit and did not succeed.

beats.scene: Ines writes a card for the wall: who is missing here
beats.summary: The club adds a new rule: ask what we are not seeing, and who is missing.

beats.scene: A grand hospital in Vienna stands under a grey sky in the year 1847
beats.summary: Ms Rao tells of a hospital in Vienna in 1847 where mothers gave birth in two clinics.

beats.scene: Two ward doors in a long corridor, one marked doctors and one midwives
beats.summary: In the clinic where doctors and students worked, far more mothers died than in the clinic run by midwives.

beats.scene: Ignaz Semmelweis crosses ideas off a long list in a notebook
beats.summary: The young doctor Ignaz Semmelweis tested ideas one by one and ruled out crowding, the position of the mothers and more.

beats.scene: A doctor sits beside the bed of his sick friend in a dim room
beats.summary: In 1847 Semmelweis's friend Jakob Kolletschka died after a cut from a scalpel during an autopsy, with symptoms like the mothers' fever.

beats.scene: Students in dark coats walk straight from the dissecting room to the ward
beats.summary: Doctors and students in the first clinic went straight from examining dead bodies to examining mothers, but the midwives did not.

beats.scene: Semmelweis writes if hands are clean, fewer mothers will die on a card
beats.summary: Semmelweis made a prediction: if the doctors washed their hands, fewer mothers would die.

beats.scene: A chart shows a tall line of deaths dropping sharply after May 1847
beats.summary: In the months after handwashing began, deaths in the doctors' clinic fell sharply, to about the level of the midwives' clinic.

beats.scene: Colleagues in black coats turn away from a chart held out by Semmelweis
beats.summary: Many doctors rejected his results, and it took time and more evidence for handwashing to be accepted.

beats.scene: A surgeon sprays carbolic acid over an operating table in the 1860s
beats.summary: In the 1860s Pasteur's work on germs and Lister's clean surgery explained why washing works, but Semmelweis died in 1865.

beats.scene: Ines and Dev wash their hands at the school sink before lunch
beats.summary: Ines and Dev wash their hands and agree that evidence must be explained clearly and kindly as well as shown.

beats.scene: An old painting shows mice crawling out of a sack of grain
beats.summary: For centuries many people believed that mice, maggots and tiny creatures could appear from nothing.

beats.scene: Three jars of meat: one open, one sealed, one covered with cloth
beats.summary: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in open, sealed and cloth-covered jars, and maggots grew only where flies could land.

beats.scene: A man peers through a tiny hand-made lens at a drop of pond water
beats.summary: In the 1670s Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw tiny living things in water, which raised the question of where microbes come from.

beats.scene: Louis Pasteur bends a glass tube over a flame in his laboratory
beats.summary: Pasteur needed a test in which broth could breathe fresh air, to answer critics who said sealed flasks spoiled the experiment.

beats.scene: Two glass flasks, one with a long curved neck, stand on a laboratory shelf
beats.summary: In the 1860s Louis Pasteur used flasks with curved necks to show that microbes come from other microbes.

beats.scene: A tilted flask lets the broth reach the dusty bend in its neck
beats.summary: When a flask was tilted so that broth touched the dust in the neck, it soon clouded, which showed that the dust carried the germs.

beats.scene: Two scientists argue politely across a table covered with glass flasks
beats.summary: Pasteur's opponent Felix Pouchet argued back, and the dispute was settled by better experiments, not by shouting.

beats.scene: Three bread slices: in an open dish, a sealed bag, a damp bag
beats.summary: The club tests mould on bread in three conditions: open to the air, sealed in a bag, and sealed with a damp cloth.

beats.scene: Fuzzy green mould grows on a slice of bread inside a sealed bag
beats.summary: Mould grew on all the slices, even in the sealed bags, because the bread already held spores, so the test was weaker than Pasteur's.

beats.scene: Clean sealed jars of preserved fruit stand in a row on a kitchen shelf
beats.summary: Knowing that germs come from germs led to safer food, pasteurised milk and cleaner medicine.

beats.scene: Ms Rao draws a circle on the whiteboard and writes Earth inside it
beats.summary: Ms Rao asks whether the club could measure the whole Earth from the school field, and notes that the Greeks knew it was round.

beats.scene: Eratosthenes reads scrolls among tall shelves in the great library of Alexandria
beats.summary: About 240 BC Eratosthenes, a librarian in Alexandria, read that in Syene the Sun lit the bottom of a well at noon on midsummer's day.

beats.scene: A tall stick casts a short shadow on the sunlit ground of Alexandria
beats.summary: On the same day in Alexandria a stick still cast a shadow, so the Sun was not overhead there.

beats.scene: Sticks cast matching shadows on a flat board, different ones on a ball
beats.summary: On a flat Earth with a faraway Sun, shadows would match; different shadows show that the surface is curved.

beats.scene: A circle is divided into fifty slices with one slice shaded

On Thursday afternoon, four children gather in the science room: Ines, Dev and two friends called Amara and Tomas. Ms Rao writes the words Question Club on the whiteboard in bright blue.
Ms Rao holds up a thick textbook and says that science is not only the facts inside it. Science, she explains, is a careful way of finding out what is true, and anyone can learn its habits.
Ms Rao writes two rules on the whiteboard, underneath the name of the club. The first is to ask how we know, and the second is to say I might be wrong when we are not sure.

The next Thursday, the children bring back their notebooks. Ms Rao shows them how a scientist writes: the date, the place, the weather, and then only what was really seen.
The first habit is to look closely and write down what you really see. Ines notices small holes in a leaf, and she counts them instead of just saying the leaf is damaged.

Ms Rao asks them to draw two columns, one for what they see and one for what they think. That the leaf has twenty-three holes goes in the first column, while the guess about hungry insects goes in the second.
Tomas says at once that bugs made the holes, and he sounds very sure. Ms Rao asks him politely whether he saw a bug, or whether he only thinks there must have been one.
Ms Rao takes the club outside for a walk around the school field. They find ants, a grey feather and a long puddle, and each child writes a different list.
Amara kneels beside the ant trail and starts a stopwatch. She counts 41 ants passing one spot in a minute and writes the number down, because a number is better than saying lots.
Ms Rao sets out three bowls of water, one cold, one warm and one pleasantly hot. A hand from the cold bowl feels the warm water as hot, while a hand from the hot bowl feels it as cold.
Ms Rao draws two lines with arrowheads on the board, and one looks clearly longer. Ines measures them with a ruler, and to everyone's surprise they are exactly the same length.

The two pupils are called Priya and Joel, and they are a year older than the club. Their numbers differ a little from Amara's, but the pattern is the same, so they join the Question Club.
Ms Rao explains that scientists ask other laboratories to repeat important results. A discovery that only one team has ever found is exciting, but it is not yet trusted.
Ines writes the bean method as a list of steps, and Priya tries to follow it. She stops at the words some water, because nobody can repeat some, and Ines changes it to 50 millilitres.
Coach Hall agrees to lend them the football field and his clipboard. The plan is 40 penalty kicks, 20 in the lucky socks and 20 in plain white ones.
Before the test, the club agrees what counts as a save and where the ball must be placed. Deciding the rules in advance stops anyone from changing them to get a better result.
Before each block of five kicks, the club draws a slip from a hat to choose Dev's socks. Chance decides the order, so tiredness and the time of day do not favour either pair.
On a cold Saturday morning, Dev faces his 40 penalty kicks. Ines records every kick, even the ones she would rather forget.
Dev saves eight of 20 kicks in the lucky socks and seven of 20 in the plain ones. The difference is so small that chance could easily explain it.
Dev sits quietly on the grass and holds his lucky socks in both hands. He is disappointed, but he admits that the test was fair, and that is what a good scientist must do.
A week later, Dev says that the socks still feel lucky. Ms Rao tells him that the feeling is real, but a feeling is not evidence about the world.
Ines sees a face in a cloud, and so does Dev. Human brains are so keen on finding patterns that we sometimes find them even when nothing is there.
Ms Rao hands out a sheet of dots that a computer has placed at random. The children see clusters, lines and even a bird, although the dots have no pattern at all.
In 1976 a spacecraft photographed a hill on Mars that looked like a human face. Years later, much sharper pictures showed that it was only an ordinary hill, with no face at all.
Ms Rao says that two, four, six follows a secret rule, and the club must find it. Everyone tests only numbers like eight, ten, twelve, and nobody tries a test that could prove them wrong.
Dev remembers every match he won in his lucky socks, but he forgets the ones he lost. This is called confirmation bias, because we notice what fits our beliefs.
Tomas thinks about his cousin, and a minute later his cousin phones. Ms Rao asks how many times Tomas thinks about his cousin and nothing happens.
Ms Rao hands every pupil a description that she says was written just for them. Almost everyone says it fits, but all the descriptions are exactly the same.
The club writes three ways to avoid fooling themselves. They will write predictions first, count the misses as well as the hits, and ask someone else to check their work.
Ines thinks about the day and realises something odd. The person who is easiest to fool is not a stranger but herself, and that is why careful rules matter.
Their neighbour Mr Bello says a magnetic wristband cured his backache. His story is sincere, but one story cannot show that the wristband worked.
Ines asks Mr Bello when his back began to feel better. He says it was about three weeks after he bought the band, and he gives them each a tomato.
Over the fence, Ines learns what else changed in those three weeks. Mr Bello rested more, bought a new chair and enjoyed warm weather, and any of these could have helped.
Ms Rao draws a line of pain that goes up and down over weeks. People try a new cure when the pain is at its worst, and then the pain often improves anyway.
Tomas says his aunt wore a similar band and felt nothing, but she never told anyone. We mostly hear stories from the people who feel better, and rarely from the others.
Amara brings in adverts from magazines, each full of happy customers' words. Nobody can check who these people are, or how many others tried the product and got nothing.
Tomas says his uncle never wore a seat belt and lived to be 90. Studies of huge numbers of crashes show that seat belts save lives, so one lucky uncle does not change the answer.
Ines sketches a test with two groups of people, one wearing the band and one not. Ms Rao says it is a good start, but she asks what might be wrong with it.
Ines worries that her questions might hurt Mr Bello's feelings. Ms Rao tells her that kindness and curiosity go together, because asking carefully is a way of taking someone's story seriously.
Ines writes a note at the top of a fresh page: ask Mr Bello when I know how. She does not want to ask until she can offer him a proper, fair way to find out.
A placebo is a pretend treatment, such as a sugar pill. Some people feel better after taking one, because they expect it to help, which is why doctors must test new medicines against it.
Ms Rao explains that a dummy pill can change how we feel, especially pain and tiredness. It cannot mend a broken bone, so we must also measure what really changes.
Ms Rao pours the same juice into two cups, one with a fancy label and one with a plain label. Most of the club says that the fancy one tastes better, even though it is exactly the same.
Ines draws two circles, one for people who get the real treatment and one for people who get a dummy. The only difference between the groups is what is in the pill.
In a blind test, people do not know whether they are receiving the real treatment or the dummy. In a double-blind test, the researchers do not know either, so no one's hopes can affect the result.
About 1900, a German horse called Clever Hans seemed to solve sums by tapping his hoof. A careful investigator found that the horse was reading tiny signals from the people near him.

In 1784, a French committee that included Benjamin Franklin tested a healer's claim of a magnetic force. They blindfolded the patients and found that people reacted to what they believed, not to what was done.
Tomas says that he can taste the difference between tap and bottled water. With his eyes closed and the cups coded, he gets only four out of eight right.
To make two fair groups, the club draws names from a bag. If people chose their own group, the keen ones might all end up together, and the test would be unfair.

That evening, Ines carefully redraws her plan for testing Mr Bello's wristband. The bands look identical, the groups are chosen by chance, nobody knows who wears which, and everyone scores their pain each day.
In the 1700s, scurvy killed huge numbers of sailors on long voyages. They became weak and tired, their gums bled, and old wounds opened again.
Some doctors recommended fresh air, others vinegar, and others a daily cup of sea water. Each cure had a few happy stories, but nobody had compared them fairly.
In 1747, James Lind is a naval surgeon on the ship Salisbury. When scurvy spreads among the crew, he decides to test the popular cures instead of arguing about them.
Lind chooses twelve sailors with scurvy, whose symptoms are as alike as he can find. They sleep in the same part of the ship and eat the same food.
Lind divides the men into six pairs, and each pair gets a different treatment. One pair has cider, one has vinegar, and one drinks a little sea water.
Dev points out that Lind changed only one thing, the treatment, and kept the rest the same. That is what makes his test fair, just like the pots of beans.
After about six days, one of the sailors who ate the oranges and lemons is fit for duty. The other has recovered so well that he can look after the sick men.
Ms Rao reminds the club that twelve sailors is a very small sample, and Lind could not be completely sure. Even so, the careful design made the result more convincing than any single story.
Lind published his results in 1753, but the navy waited until the 1790s to give sailors lemon juice. Scientists found the real cause, a lack of vitamin C, much later.
Walking home, Dev peels an orange and says that twelve sailors did more good than a thousand opinions. Ines agrees, but she wonders what happens when a fair test is not possible.
In summer, ice cream sales go up, and so do accidents in the water. This does not mean that ice cream causes accidents, because hot weather makes more people do both.
Amara shows that children with bigger feet score higher in reading tests. Big feet do not help reading, because older children have both bigger feet and more practice.
Scientists call a hidden third factor a confounder, and it can fool us. People who carry lighters are more likely to get lung disease, but the true cause is smoking, which the lighters are linked to.
Dev notes that team captains score more goals, but Ms Rao asks which comes first. Perhaps good players are chosen as captains, instead of captains becoming good players.
A statistician once showed that European countries with more storks also have more babies. Storks do not bring babies, because bigger countries simply have more of everything.
Amara pins up two jagged lines that rise and fall together, and they come from two silly lists of numbers. If you compare thousands of pairs of numbers, some pairs will match by pure chance.
When scientists can run an experiment, they choose the groups by chance. Then hidden factors like age and weather are spread evenly, and a real difference is more likely to come from the treatment.

Nobody can ask people to start smoking, so scientists cannot test it as an experiment. In the 1950s, British researchers followed tens of thousands of doctors for years and compared those who smoked with those who did not.
Ms Rao lists three signs of a real cause. Many different studies point the same way, the cause comes before the effect, and there is a believable reason for how it works.
The club writes a rule on the wall, which says that linked does not mean caused. Whenever they hear that one thing is linked to another, they will ask what else could explain it.
Ms Rao draws a plane and marks red dots where returning planes were hit in the Second World War. She asks the club where extra armour should go.
Tomas says at once that armour should go where the holes are. Ms Rao asks him a quiet question: which planes are we looking at, and which ones are missing?
A mathematician named Abraham Wald, working with a group of statisticians in New York, saw the trick. The holes showed where a plane could be hit and still fly home.
So the strongest armour should go where the returning planes have no holes, such as around the engines. Planes hit there did not come back to be counted.
Ms Rao admits that the tidy story is simplified. The real Wald wrote pages of difficult calculations to estimate how likely a plane was to survive a hit in each part.
Ms Rao writes the words survivorship bias on the board and underlines them twice. It means that when we look only at what survived, we can draw the wrong conclusion about everything.
Amara says that old buildings are lovely and strong, and new ones are ugly. Ms Rao points out that the weak, ugly old buildings were pulled down long ago, so we only see the survivors.
Dev asks his teammates whether football is fun, and every one of them says yes. Then Ines asks about the children who left the team, and nobody has asked them.
Tomas reads a magazine story about a rich person who left school early and made a fortune. Ms Rao asks about the thousands who left school and did not, because nobody writes stories about them.
The club pins a new rule beside the others. It says to ask what you are not seeing, and who is missing from the picture.
Ms Rao tells the club about a large hospital in Vienna in the year 1847. Mothers there had their babies in one of two clinics, and handwashing was not yet a usual habit.
In one clinic, doctors and medical students look after the mothers, and in the other, midwives do. Far more mothers die in the doctors' clinic, and nobody knows why.

A young Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis tests one idea after another. The second clinic is more crowded, not less, so crowding cannot explain it, and the way the mothers lie makes no difference either.
In 1847, Semmelweis's friend Jakob Kolletschka cuts his finger with a scalpel while examining a dead body. He dies of an illness that looks just like the mothers' fever.
Semmelweis notices that the doctors and students often work with dead bodies and then go straight to the mothers. The midwives never do this work, and their clinic has fewer deaths.
Semmelweis makes a prediction: if the doctors clean their hands, fewer mothers will die. In May 1847 he orders everyone to wash in a strong chlorine solution before entering the ward.
In the months after the handwashing began, deaths in the doctors' clinic fell sharply. Soon they were about as low as in the midwives' clinic.
Many doctors rejected the idea of handwashing, partly because they did not like to be told that they had caused harm. Only later, with more evidence about germs, did the practice become accepted.
In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur's work on germs and Joseph Lister's clean surgery explained why washing works. Semmelweis died in 1865, before most doctors had accepted his idea.
Before lunch, Dev and Ines wash their hands carefully at the school sink. They talk about how Semmelweis was right but could not persuade people, and they decide that evidence needs kindness too.
For centuries, many people believed that living things could appear from nothing. They thought that maggots came from rotting meat, and that mice came from dirty rags and grain.
In 1668, an Italian doctor named Francesco Redi put meat in three jars, one open, one sealed and one covered with fine cloth. Maggots appeared only on the meat that flies could reach.

In the 1670s, a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made tiny lenses and looked at pond water. He saw a crowd of tiny living things, and the old question came back: where do they come from?
Pasteur's critics say that a sealed flask has no fresh air, so nothing can grow in it. He needs a flask that lets in air but keeps out the dust.
In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks. Air could enter but dust was trapped, and the broth stayed clear, showing that germs come from other germs.
Pasteur tilts one flask so that the broth flows into the curved neck, where the dust is trapped. Soon the broth turns cloudy, because dust has carried microbes into it from the neck.
Pasteur's chief opponent, Felix Pouchet, does not give up at once. The argument is settled by more experiments, and in the end almost all scientists agree with Pasteur.
Three slices of bread are set out: one in an open dish, one in a sealed bag and one in a damp bag. Ms Rao makes everyone promise never to open the sealed bags.
After a week, fuzzy mould grows on all three slices, even in the sealed bags. Tomas is surprised, until Ms Rao explains that the bread was never heated, so some spores were already on it.
Knowing that germs come from other germs changed the world. It led to pasteurised milk, cleaner hospitals and safer food, and it explained why Semmelweis's handwashing worked.
Ms Rao asks whether the club could measure the whole Earth from the school field. Long ago, she says, people already knew that the Earth is round, because ships disappear hull first over the horizon.

About 240 BC, a Greek scholar named Eratosthenes worked in the great library of Alexandria in Egypt. He read that on one day each summer, the noon Sun shone straight down a deep well in a town called Syene.
On that same day in Alexandria, Eratosthenes puts a stick upright in the ground. It still casts a short shadow, so the Sun is not straight overhead there.
Ms Rao stands two sticks on a flat board and shines a torch from far away, and the shadows match. On a ball, the two shadows are different, and the same must be true on the Earth.

Eratosthenes measured the angle of the shadow, which was about one fiftieth of a full circle. The two towns were about 5,000 stadia apart, so the whole Earth must be fifty times as big around, or about 250,000 stadia.
Nobody is certain how long a stadion was, so historians disagree about his accuracy. His answer was either very close to the true size, or too big by about a sixth.
Ms Rao phones her friend Mr Silva, who teaches in a town about 300 kilometres to the north. They agree that both classes will measure a noon shadow on the same day.
On the chosen day, the club watches the shadow of a one-metre stick shrink until it is shortest. Amara marks the end with chalk, while Mr Silva's class does the same far away.
A scale drawing of the two shadows shows that the Sun's angles differ by about three degrees. Three degrees is one 120th of a full circle, so the Earth must be about 36,000 kilometres around.
The real distance around the Earth is about 40,000 kilometres, so the club is about a tenth too small. Ms Rao says that is wonderful, because a blurry shadow edge can easily cause that much error.
Ms Rao tells a story about a prediction that was so risky it could have ended a famous idea. For more than 200 years, Isaac Newton's theory of gravity had worked beautifully.
Einstein's theory said that the Sun's gravity would bend the path of starlight passing close to it. The bend would be tiny, but about twice as big as the old theory suggested.
There was a problem, because the stars near the Sun cannot be seen in bright daylight. Only during a total eclipse, when the Moon covers the Sun, does the sky grow dark enough.
The plan is to photograph the stars near the eclipsed Sun, and then to compare them with photographs of the same stars taken at night. If the stars have moved, the light was bent.
A total eclipse was due on 29 May 1919, so two teams of scientists set out to watch it. Arthur Eddington went to the island of Principe, and another team went to Sobral in Brazil.
On the morning of the eclipse, heavy rain falls on Principe, and the team fears the worst. Shortly before the eclipse begins, the clouds thin, and Eddington's team takes the photographs they can.
Back home, the team spends weeks measuring tiny distances on the glass plates. At Sobral, heat has blurred the images of one telescope, so they must decide carefully how much to trust it.
In November 1919, the results were announced to a meeting in London. The starlight had bent by about the amount that Einstein had predicted, and newspapers called it a revolution in science.
The important point is that the test could have failed. A risky prediction that passes a fair test is much stronger evidence than a safe one that nothing could contradict.
Ms Rao says that scientists accept what a test shows, even about their own ideas. Ines writes a new question at the top of her page: what would show me that I am wrong?
Dev says there is an invisible cat in the room that makes no sound and cannot be touched. Ms Rao says that an idea nothing could ever disprove is not useful, because it explains nothing at all.
Tomas sprinkles flour on the floor to catch paw prints, but Dev says the cat floats. He tries a bell and a sniff next, and every time Dev has a new reason why the test fails.
Ms Rao explains that the invisible cat is not wrong, but empty. A useful idea has to say what we should not see, so that some result could show it is false.

For centuries, Europeans believed that all swans are white, which was a clear idea that could be tested. In 1697 a Dutch explorer saw black swans in Western Australia, and one black swan was enough to prove it wrong.
Tomas says his grandfather uses a forked stick to find water under the ground. When the stick fails, he says that someone in the group was doubting, which means that it can never fail.
A friend says he saw a cat in the street, and you believe him easily. If he says he saw a cat fly, you would want much better proof, because the claim is so much bigger.
When someone makes a claim, it is up to that person to show the evidence. It is not up to everyone else to prove the claim wrong.
The biscuits have vanished, and there are crumbs on the dog's bed. The simplest explanation is that the dog took them, so that is the one the children test before they think of anything more exotic.
The club gathers its rules on one wall as a toolkit of questions. What did we see, what else could explain it, what would show it wrong, and how strong is the evidence?
Dev says that perhaps the invisible cat is real and just very shy. Ines laughs and answers that it could be, but then it cannot count as evidence for anything.
When you read a claim, ask who is saying it and how they know. Also ask whether the person will earn money or fame if you believe it.
Ines follows the links on the page, and each one leads to another page on the same website. At last she finds a shop that sells the food, and no real study at all.

An advert shows a famous actor in a white coat, who says that a vitamin drink will make you strong. Being good at acting does not make someone an expert on health, so Ines asks what the actor has studied.
People who have studied a subject for many years deserve our attention. Good experts explain their reasons, and when almost all of them agree, that is strong evidence.
In 1912, Alfred Wegener said that the continents slowly move, and most experts rejected the idea. In the 1960s, new evidence from the sea floor changed their minds.
Before most scientific studies are published, other experts read them and look for mistakes. This is called peer review, and it is a useful filter, though it is not perfect.
In 2015, a large team of researchers repeated 100 psychology studies. Fewer than half gave the same clear result, which showed that some studies were weaker than they had seemed.
A headline says that something doubles your risk of an illness. If the risk was one in a million, it is now two in a million, and that is still very small.
Ms Rao draws the same numbers on two graphs. On one, the axis starts high, so a small change looks huge, and on the other it starts at zero and the change looks small.

Cherry picking means showing only the facts that support your side and leaving out the rest. Dev did this when he counted only the wins in his lucky socks, and a careful thinker looks at all the evidence.
In everyday speech, people say theory when they mean a guess. In science, a theory is an explanation that has been tested many times and that fits a great deal of evidence.
Ms Rao puts three words on the board: fact, law and theory. A fact is something we observe, a law describes a pattern, and a theory explains why the pattern happens.
A weather forecast says there is a seventy per cent chance of rain. A scientist is not weak for saying this, because being honest about uncertainty is a sign of careful work.
Amara learns to write her bean heights with a margin, such as 63 millimetres, give or take two. The margin shows how far the number can be trusted, and it makes the report more honest.
When Dev asks a hard question, Ms Rao says honestly that she does not know the answer. Saying I do not know is the start of finding out, and it is nothing to be ashamed of.

Ines had always believed that cold air gives you a cold, but she reads that colds are caused by viruses. She crosses out her old note, and she adds that in winter we spend more time close together indoors.
A seller promises a miracle tonic that cures everything, using only happy stories and a secret recipe. These are warning signs, because real treatments are tested openly.
Ms Rao hands out a pretend advert for Sparkle Tonic, a drink that cures every illness. The club finds a secret recipe, happy customer stories, no test and a very high price.
Ms Rao says that real science invites tests and changes when the evidence changes. Pseudoscience avoids tests, protects its ideas and keeps its claims the same, whatever happens.
Dev finds a dramatic photo online and wants to share it. Ines says to check where it came from first, because pictures can be edited, old or from a different event.
We are most easily fooled when we badly want something to be true. Ms Rao says that a strong feeling is a good signal to slow down and check the facts twice.
Ines gets a forwarded message saying that school is closed tomorrow. Although she badly wants it to be true, she checks the school's own website first, and the message is false.
Ines disagrees with Dev about a result, and they argue about the evidence in a friendly way. Ms Rao reminds them to challenge the idea and not the person.

Ines notices that nobody in the club has ever been laughed at for a wrong guess, not Tomas, not Dev and not herself. Ms Rao says that a good club is a place where it is safe to be wrong, and then to try again.
Lying on the grass at night, the friends look at the stars. Knowing how stars shine and how far away they are does not spoil the view, and it makes it even more amazing.
For their final project, the club asks whether music helps people remember words. They plan two groups, one quiet and one with music, and choose who goes where by drawing names from a bag.
The club asks twenty classmates to learn a list of words, half in silence and half with music. The silent group remembers slightly more words, but the sample is small, so the club cannot be sure.
Ms Rao reads Ines's plan for testing the wristband and says that it is a fair one. She advises her to ask Mr Bello as a friend, not as a judge.
Dev still wears his lucky socks before every match, because they make him feel happy. He knows now that his skill wins the games, and not the socks.
Ines visits Mr Bello and asks him kindly how he could know that the wristband works. She is not trying to win an argument, only to help them both find out.
C1C2: Before every football match, Dev put on a pair of striped socks that he swore were lucky, and he had a long list of the times his team had won while he wore them. Ines, who had never been able to leave a claim alone, asked him quietly how he could actually know the socks were doing anything. It was the question that would carry them through the whole term, and it is one worth asking about nearly everything.

Dev carried a crumpled list in his school bag, and on it he had written the date of every match his team had won since September. Beside each date was the same two words, striped socks, written in blue pen and underlined twice. Ines read the list carefully, and although she admired his handwriting, a small question was already forming in her mind.

On Saturday the team won by two goals to one, and Dev, who had made three fine saves, was lifted onto the shoulders of his friends. He pointed proudly at his striped socks and announced that the proof was now beyond argument. Ines, standing by the fence with her notebook, smiled politely and wondered what kind of proof it really was.

On Monday morning a bright poster appeared on the school noticeboard, drawn in blue marker with a large question mark in the middle. Ms Rao, the science teacher, was starting a club for children who liked to ask questions, and it would meet every Thursday after lessons. Ines read the poster twice, and then she dragged Dev over to read it too.

On the way home, the two friends passed the garden of Mr Bello, a retired bus driver who spent most of his days among his tomato plants. He waved to them with the arm that wore a shiny metal band, a magnetic wristband that he was happy to show to anyone who asked. Ines waved back, and without quite knowing why, she found herself looking at the band for a long time.

On Thursday afternoon four children gathered in the science room, which smelled faintly of chalk and warm plastic. Besides Ines and Dev there were Amara, a quiet girl who drew in the margin of everything, and Tomas, a cheerful boy who could not stop talking. Ms Rao picked up a blue marker and wrote the words Question Club across the whiteboard in letters a foot tall.

Ms Rao held up a thick textbook and told the club that science was not a heap of facts to be memorised. It was, she said, a careful way of finding out what is true, built from habits that anyone could learn. Those habits would be useful, she promised, long after they had forgotten the names of the planets.

Underneath the name of the club, Ms Rao wrote two rules that she said would matter more than any fact. The first was to ask, of every claim, how we know it, and the second was to be brave enough to say that we might be wrong. Dev read them aloud, and Ines felt that someone had at last put her favourite question on a whiteboard.

To start, Ms Rao placed a sealed shoebox on the table and asked the children to discover what was inside without opening it. They were allowed to shake it, tilt it, weigh it and listen to it, and they soon began to argue happily about what each sound might mean. Tomas insisted that it rattled like a bag of marbles, whereas Amara thought it rolled more like a pencil.

At last Ms Rao lifted the lid, and inside lay a small toy car and a pencil, which meant that Tomas and Amara had each been partly right. A careful guess, she told them, is a perfectly respectable beginning, but it only becomes knowledge once something has been checked. Before they left, she handed each child a blank notebook and asked them to bring it back the next Thursday with something interesting noticed inside.

The following Thursday the children returned with their notebooks, and Ms Rao spent the first ten minutes showing them how a scientist keeps one. Every entry should carry the date, the place and the weather, followed by what was really seen, in plain words and with numbers wherever possible. Tomas, whose notebook was half full of doodles of rockets, admitted that he had some work to do.

The first habit, Ms Rao said, is to observe carefully, and to record what you actually see rather than what you expect or hope to see. Ines held a leaf under a magnifying glass, noticed that it was full of tiny holes, and counted twenty-three of them instead of just announcing that it looked damaged. A number can be checked by another person, whereas an impression cannot, and that is why scientists prefer to count and measure.

Ms Rao asked the children to draw a line down the middle of the page, with what we see on the left and what we think on the right. The number of holes belonged on the left, because anyone could check it, whereas the guess about hungry insects belonged firmly on the right. Mixing the two columns, she warned, is how a good observation quietly turns into a bad argument.

Tomas declared at once that bugs had made the holes, and he sounded as certain as if he had watched them do it. Ms Rao asked him, with a gentle smile, whether he had actually seen a bug or merely believed there must have been one. Tomas admitted that it was the second, and he moved his sentence carefully into the right-hand column.

Ms Rao led the club out onto the school field for a notebook walk, and they spread out along the hedge like a small expedition. Within ten minutes they had found an ant trail, a grey feather, a snail shell and a puddle shaped like a boot. What astonished Ines was that all four of them had written different lists, although they had walked the same path.

Amara knelt beside the ant trail, started the stopwatch on her wrist, and counted how many ants crossed one crack in the path during a single minute. There were 41, and she wrote the number in her notebook beside the time and the temperature of the morning. Later, when she counted again, she got 38, which taught her that even careful counting leaves a small margin of error.

Ms Rao set out three bowls of water, one cold, one lukewarm and one comfortably hot, and she asked everyone to rest one hand in each of the outer bowls for a minute. When the children moved both hands into the lukewarm bowl, it felt warm to the hand that had been cold and cool to the hand that had been hot. Our senses, she concluded, are wonderful tools, but they compare things with a moment ago, so a thermometer is a better witness.

On the whiteboard Ms Rao drew two straight lines, one with its arrowheads pointing in and the other with its arrowheads pointing out. Every child in the room was certain that one of the lines was longer, until Ines fetched a ruler and showed that the two were precisely equal. Knowing the trick did not stop the illusion, Ms Rao added, so measuring is the only way to trust what we see.

Ms Rao asked Dev to write down, from memory, everything that had happened in last Saturday's match. Afterwards Ines compared his account with a short video that Coach Hall had filmed, and it turned out that Dev had put two of the goals in the wrong order and credited the wrong player with one of them. Memory, Ms Rao said kindly, is not a recording but a story that we rebuild every time we tell it, which is exactly why scientists write things down at the time.

By the end of the meeting Ines had filled three whole pages, and the strange thing was that every observation had produced a new question. Why did the ants follow one path, why did the leaf have holes only at its edge, and why did her own memory differ from the video? Ms Rao smiled when she saw the page, because noticing, she said, is where every investigation begins.

Dev asked why the holes in the leaf looked so ugly, but Ms Rao pointed out that this was a matter of taste, not of evidence, and that nobody could settle it with an experiment. A better question, she suggested, would be what had made the holes, because that has an answer that can be found by looking and testing. Scientists spend a good deal of their time turning big, vague puzzles into small questions of this kind.

Ms Rao wrote six questions on the whiteboard and asked the club to sort them into those that science could answer and those that it could not. Whether chocolate is better than vanilla was a matter of taste, which no experiment could settle, but whether plants grow taller in sunlight was something anyone could test. Some questions, she observed, are lovely to argue about, while others are lovely to investigate, and it helps to know which kind you are holding.

Tomas asked whether plants grow better when music is playing, and Ms Rao said that it was a charming question but not yet a testable one. What did better mean, she asked, and how would he measure it, in height, in number of leaves, or in weight after a month of growing? A good question, she explained, is one that points to something you can count or measure.

Before choosing a favourite, Ines made a list of everything that could have made the holes, and the list grew to four suspects: a caterpillar, a snail, a shower of hailstones and a gardener with a hole punch. Ms Rao approved of the last one because it was silly but still testable, and she pointed out that each suspect would leave different clues behind. Careful thinkers, she said, keep several explanations alive for as long as they possibly can, and they let the evidence choose between them.

Ines wrote on a card, Caterpillars made the holes, and pinned it beside the leaf. A guess of this kind is called a hypothesis, and what makes it scientific is that the facts could show it to be wrong, since the leaf might turn out to have been damaged by wind or by something else. An idea that nothing could ever contradict, Ms Rao said, might be comforting, but it would not teach us anything.

If the hypothesis was right, Ms Rao explained, then certain other things ought to be true as well, and that gives you a chance to check. Ines predicted that she would find a caterpillar, a chewed edge or a scattering of tiny droppings on the plant, and she went outside to look. Making a prediction before you look is a way of keeping yourself honest, because it stops you from explaining away whatever you happen to find.

Outside, Ines turned the leaves over one by one, trying hard not to hope too much. Under the fourth one she found a small green caterpillar, still chewing, and below it a scatter of tiny black droppings, exactly as her prediction had said. She wrote down the date, the time and the position of the plant before she allowed herself to smile.

Tomas wanted to declare the mystery solved and go home, but Ms Rao asked what else might explain the caterpillar and the droppings. Perhaps a snail had visited the plant earlier, or perhaps the caterpillar had arrived after the holes were made. Evidence, she said, usually supports an idea to some degree rather than proving it, so scientists speak of how strong the support is.

Dev took a fresh card and wrote his belief in a form that could be tested, namely that he saved more penalty kicks when he wore the lucky socks. Ms Rao was delighted, because the sentence was clear and specific, and the facts could show it to be wrong. Dev read it again, swallowed, and said that he supposed that was the point.

Dev confessed to Ines on the way out that he was a little nervous, because the test might show that his socks did nothing at all. Then he squared his shoulders and said that if they did nothing, he would rather know than go on guessing. Ms Rao, who had overheard, told them both that this was a very scientific thing to say, and that the next job was to learn what makes a test fair.

Ms Rao brought in a bag of dried beans, four small pots and a sack of compost, and she let the beans soak overnight in a bowl of water. The next day the children sorted through them, setting aside any that were cracked, shrivelled or noticeably larger than the rest. Choosing carefully at the start, she told them, saves a great deal of confusion at the end.

Tomas proudly set up his own version of the test, with one bean in rich compost on the windowsill and another in sand inside the cupboard. Ines pointed out that if the two plants grew differently, nobody could say whether the light, the soil or the water was responsible, because several things had changed at once. Tomas looked at his two pots, laughed out loud, and began to unpick his own experiment before anyone else could.

The club decided to test whether light matters to a growing bean, so they planted two identical pots with the same soil, the same amount of water and the same warmth. One pot went onto the sunny windowsill and the other into a dark cupboard, so that light was the only thing that differed between them. A fair test, Ms Rao reminded them, changes one thing at a time, since otherwise you could never tell which change was responsible for the result.

Ms Rao introduced some useful words, explaining that anything that can change in an experiment is called a variable, and that a good test changes only one while it measures another and keeps all the rest steady. A control is a comparison, a version of the experiment in which the thing being tested is left out, so that its effect can be seen by contrast. Without something to compare against, a result of any kind can say very little.

Amara planted three beans in each pot instead of one, because a single seed might be dud or unlucky, and a result built on one seed would be fragile. She labelled the pots with the date, the place and the names of the planters in her small, tidy writing. Dev watched her work and thought that she was building the test the way a careful builder lays bricks.

Every afternoon Ines measured the height of each shoot with a ruler, and Dev recorded the numbers in a table that grew longer by the day. It would have been easy simply to say that the sunny plant looked healthier, but looks are influenced by hopes and moods, whereas a measurement in millimetres is something that a stranger could repeat. Putting numbers on things, Ms Rao said, is one of the simplest and most powerful tricks in science.

After a week of measuring, Amara turned the long table of numbers into a graph, with one coloured line for the window pot and another for the cupboard pot. A pattern that had been hidden among dozens of figures leapt out as soon as it became a picture. Ms Rao admired the axes, which Amara had labelled with units, and said that a graph without labels is just a pretty drawing.

One Wednesday the school caretaker, who had meant to be kind, gave the cupboard pot an extra cup of water. Ines was upset at first, but Ms Rao told her to write the mistake in the notebook rather than hide it, because a slip that is recorded can be taken into account. A scientist who hides an error spoils the work, whereas one who confesses it makes the work more trustworthy.

To everyone's surprise, the beans in the dark cupboard grew taller than the ones on the windowsill, after only ten days. Looking closer, the children saw that the tall plants were thin, pale and floppy, whereas the plants in the window were short, sturdy and deep green. Plants kept in the dark, Ms Rao explained, stretch fast to search for light, but with no light they cannot make food and they weaken.

Ines had written down a prediction before the test, saying that the sunny beans would grow tallest, and now the evidence had proved her wrong. She felt a small sting, and then something better, which was curiosity about why the plants behaved so strangely. Because she had committed herself in advance, Ms Rao said, she could not pretend afterwards that she had expected it all along, and that honesty is the heart of the method.

Ms Rao flipped a coin four times and got three heads, and she asked whether the coin was unfair. Dev said it probably was, but she explained that such a small number of flips can easily produce a lopsided result by chance alone, whereas four hundred flips would give a count very close to two hundred of each. The more trials or people an experiment includes, the less likely it is that a fluke has fooled us.

Each of the four children tossed a coin ten times and marked the results on a tally sheet. Ines got seven heads, Dev got four, Amara got five and Tomas got six, even though all four coins were perfectly fair. Nobody had cheated, Ms Rao said, because variety is simply what chance looks like in a small group.

Ms Rao then collected the tallies from the whole class next door, and the club added them up on the board, making 200 tosses in all. The total was 104 heads and 96 tails, which is remarkably close to an even split, although no single child had come out exactly even. The pattern that was invisible in ten tosses had appeared in two hundred, and this, Ms Rao said, is why scientists like large numbers.

Amara wished to discover which school lunch was the most popular, and her first instinct was to consult her two closest friends. Ms Rao pointed out that two people from the same table could easily share the same taste, whereas 50 pupils from every year would provide a far more reliable picture of the whole school. The people you ask are called a sample, she explained, and a good sample is both large enough and chosen fairly.

The club rolled a die 60 times and counted how often each number came up, expecting about ten of each. The graph that Amara drew was wobbly instead of flat, with the five appearing 14 times and the two only six times, even though the die was perfectly fair. Chance, Ms Rao said, never delivers the tidy numbers we imagine, so a small wobble is no evidence that something is wrong.

Ines noticed that even the two beans in the same sunny pot did not grow by exactly the same amount, and Ms Rao said that this was entirely normal. Chance, in the form of small differences in the seeds, the soil and the weather, always makes results wobble a little, so scientists take many measurements and look at the average. What matters is whether the difference between the groups is clearly bigger than the wobble.

When Ines and Amara measured the very same bean shoot, Ines got 62 millimetres and Amara got 64. Neither girl had made a mistake in the ordinary sense, since the tip of a shoot is soft, the ruler is thick and every measurement carries a small error of its own. The trick, Ms Rao said, is to measure more than once and to be honest about the wobble.

Ms Rao showed the club how to find an average, by adding up several measurements and dividing the total by how many there were. The average of 62, 64 and 63 millimetres was 63, a figure that was steadier and fairer than any one of them alone. Random errors tend to push some numbers up and others down, she explained, so they partly cancel each other out when we combine the results.

Dev remembered the day he saved three penalty kicks in a row while wearing his striped socks, and he offered it as strong evidence. Ms Rao explained that streaks of luck are a perfectly normal part of chance, and that even a fair coin sometimes lands heads three times running. A short run, however impressive it feels, tells us much less than a long record kept honestly.

Tomas wrote out a row of 30 coin flips from his imagination, while Ines flipped a real coin 30 times and recorded the results, and Ms Rao left the room while they hid which was which. When she returned, she identified the real row almost at once, because it contained longer streaks of heads and tails than people expect. Our minds think randomness should look evenly mixed, but real chance is clumpier than we imagine.

Two other pupils, who had not seen the first results, repeated the bean experiment in a different room, using new seeds and new pots. When they found the same pattern, everybody in the club felt far more confident than they had done after a single test, because one result could always have been a fluke. This habit of repeating experiments, sometimes by completely different teams, is called replication, and it is one of the main safeguards of science.

The two pupils turned out to be Priya and Joel, who were a year older than the club members and had been recruited by Ms Rao in the corridor. Their numbers were not identical to Amara's, since their window was shadier and their seeds came from a different packet, but the overall pattern was unmistakably the same. They were so pleased to be part of a real replication that they asked to join the club for good.

Ms Rao explained that when scientists announce a surprising discovery, other laboratories around the world try to repeat it with their own equipment.
