A result that appears once might be a fluke, a mistake or even a fraud, whereas one that appears again and again, in different hands, becomes a solid piece of knowledge. Surprising claims, she added, deserve the most checking rather than the least, because the greater the surprise, the greater the chance of a mistake.

Ines wrote out the whole bean experiment as a numbered list, like a recipe, and Priya tried to follow it without asking any questions. She got stuck at the words some water, because no one else could know how much some was, so Ines replaced them with 50 millilitres every second day. A method written clearly enough for a stranger to repeat, Ms Rao said, is a gift to every scientist who comes later.

Coach Hall agreed to lend the club the football field, a bag of balls and his clipboard, and he seemed delighted that someone was measuring things at last. The plan was for Dev to face 40 penalty kicks, 20 wearing the lucky striped socks and 20 wearing plain white ones, taken by Amara and Tomas in turn. Ms Rao insisted that every detail be fixed in writing before a single ball was kicked.

Before the test began, the club agreed on exactly what would count as a save, how far from the goal the ball would be placed and how hard the penalties could be kicked. Deciding the rules in advance, Ms Rao explained, stops everyone from quietly changing them afterwards to make the result look the way they hope. Amara wrote the rules on the whiteboard and had everyone sign underneath, rather solemnly.

To make the test fair, the club put slips of paper in a hat, and before each block of five kicks they drew one to decide which socks Dev would wear. Leaving the order to chance meant that tiredness, a gust of wind or the fading light could not favour one pair over the other. Dev, who had hoped to pick the socks himself, grumbled for a moment and then accepted that this was the whole point.

On a cold Saturday morning, with breath steaming and fingers numb, Dev crouched in the goal and faced his 40 penalty kicks. Ines recorded every single result on Coach Hall's clipboard, the saves and the goals alike, and she did not cheer when he saved one, because a recorder who cheers is a recorder who might start to hope. By the end of the long session, even Coach Hall was holding his breath before every single kick.

When the table was complete, Dev had saved eight of the 20 kicks in his striped socks and seven of the 20 in plain white ones. That is a difference of a single kick, and the coin-tossing lessons had already taught the club how easily chance can produce such a gap. The result, Ms Rao said gently, was exactly what we would expect if the socks made no difference at all.

Dev sat quietly on the damp grass for a while with the striped socks in his hands, looking oddly like someone who had lost an old friend. He was disappointed, yet he admitted to the others that the test had been fair, because he had agreed to every rule before the first ball was kicked. Admitting a result you did not want, Ms Rao told him, is the hardest and most important thing a scientist ever does.

A week later Dev admitted that, despite the result, the striped socks still felt lucky, and he could not simply switch that feeling off. Ms Rao said that the feeling was real and nothing to be ashamed of, but that a feeling about the world is not the same as evidence about it. The interesting question, she added, was why such strong feelings arise, and the club spent the next few weeks finding out.

Lying on the grass after school, Ines pointed to a cloud that looked unmistakably like a smiling face, and Dev saw it too. Human brains are tuned to spot faces and patterns, which is useful when you need to recognise a friend in a crowd, but it also means that we see meaning in random shapes, spots and coincidences. A scientist therefore learns to ask whether a pattern is real or simply something that the mind has supplied.

Ms Rao handed out a sheet of dots which, she revealed, a computer had scattered completely at random. Nevertheless the children quickly found clusters, curving lines and even a flying bird among them, and Tomas drew a ring around what he called an obvious constellation. Real randomness is lumpy, she explained, and our minds are so eager to find order that we invent it where it does not exist.

In 1976 a spacecraft in orbit around Mars photographed a hill whose shadows, under that particular light, made it look like a giant human face. The picture caused a sensation, and some people claimed that it was a monument built by a lost civilisation. Sharper photographs taken in the late 1990s and after showed an ordinary eroded hill, proving that a blurry image and an eager imagination can build a whole mystery out of nothing.

Ms Rao wrote the numbers two, four, six on the board and told the club that they obeyed a secret rule, which the children had to discover by offering other sets of three numbers. Every child guessed that the rule was adding two each time, and every child tested only sets like eight, ten, twelve that fitted the guess, hearing yes each time. The real rule, she revealed, was simply any numbers getting bigger, and nobody had thought to test an example that might have proved them wrong.

Dev could name every game that his team had won while he wore the lucky socks, but when Ines asked about the losses, he had to think hard to recall any. This is called confirmation bias, the tendency to notice and remember the evidence that supports what we already believe, and to overlook the evidence against it. The cure, Ms Rao said, is to keep a written record of the hits and the misses alike.

Tomas described the time he had been thinking about his cousin and, a minute later, the phone had rung and it was her. Ms Rao asked how many other times he had thought of his cousin without any call, and how many calls had come from people he was not thinking about. We remember the striking match and forget the countless misses, she said, and that is how ordinary coincidences come to feel like messages.

Ms Rao handed every pupil a sealed envelope containing a personal description that, she said, had been written just for them. Almost everyone agreed that it fitted them well, and then they discovered that all the descriptions were word for word the same, filled with vague lines such as you sometimes doubt yourself. Psychologists have run this very test since the 1940s, she told them, and statements that are vague enough will fit nearly anyone.

On the whiteboard the club listed three defences against their own minds, and Ines copied them into her notebook. Write the prediction down before looking, count the misses as carefully as the hits, and ask somebody else to check your work, because other people do not share your hopes. None of these rules is difficult, Ms Rao pointed out, but they are surprisingly easy to forget when you really want to be right.

Walking home, Ines thought about the clouds, the dots and the coincidences, and she came to a slightly uncomfortable conclusion. The person who is easiest for any of us to fool is not a stranger or a salesman, but ourselves, because we already want to believe what we believe. That, she decided, was exactly why scientists need rules, and why Dev's honest test had been so brave.

Mr Bello, a neighbour, told the children over the garden fence that a magnetic wristband had cured his backache, and he clearly believed every word of it. Ms Rao later explained that a personal story, or anecdote, is not worthless, but it cannot reveal whether the wristband was responsible, because backaches often improve on their own and a hundred other things may have changed that week. To judge the matter properly, you need many people, a fair comparison and a good deal of patience.

Ines asked Mr Bello, as politely as she could, when exactly his back had begun to feel better. He thought for a moment and said that it was about three weeks after he bought the band, and then he handed each of them a warm tomato from his basket. His kindness and his sincerity were obvious, and Ines felt the question growing heavier in her pocket.

By asking a few more questions over the fence, Ines found out everything else that had changed during those three weeks, and the list was longer than she expected. Mr Bello had rested more, bought a better chair, started gentle stretching and enjoyed a spell of warm weather, and any of these might have eased his back. Nothing on the list was proof of anything, Ms Rao said, but each item was a reason to be careful about crediting the band.

Ms Rao drew a wobbly line to show how pain rises and falls over a number of weeks. People tend to buy a remedy when the pain is at its very worst, she observed, and because the line usually drifts back down afterwards, the remedy gets the credit. Doctors call this a return to the average, and it fools nearly everyone at some time, including doctors themselves.

Tomas mentioned that his aunt had worn a similar band for a month and felt nothing at all, but she had never told a soul about it. The stories we hear are those of people who feel better, because nobody rushes over a garden fence to announce that something made no difference. A crowd of cheerful testimonies, Ms Rao said, can hide a far larger crowd of silent disappointments.

Amara brought in a folder of magazine adverts, each one decorated with enthusiastic quotations from satisfied customers. The club tried to find out who these customers were, how they had been chosen and how many others had tried the product and been disappointed, and the adverts did not say. A testimonial is a story with a smile on its face, Ms Rao said, and it is only as reliable as the ordinary anecdote beneath it.

Tomas protested that his uncle had never worn a seat belt in his life and had lived happily to the age of 90. Ms Rao agreed that the story was true and cheerful, but she explained that studies of huge numbers of crashes show clearly that seat belts save lives. One lucky uncle, however dear and however cheerful, is simply outweighed by thousands of careful records kept by strangers.

Ines sketched a first design for a fair test, with one group of people wearing magnetic bands and another group wearing nothing, and she planned to measure their backaches before and after. Ms Rao praised the idea of a comparison but asked what might still be wrong with it, and Ines realised that people who knew they were wearing the band might feel better simply because they expected to. She put down her pencil, because she suspected that the next lesson was going to be the answer.

Ines worried that her questions might hurt the feelings of Mr Bello, who had been so friendly to her since she was small. Ms Rao told her that kindness and curiosity are not enemies, because asking carefully is a way of taking someone's story seriously. The aim, she said, was never to win an argument or to prove anybody foolish, but to find out together what is really true.

At the top of a fresh page, Ines wrote a note to herself: ask Mr Bello, but only when I know how to help him find out. She did not want to leave him with doubts and no answers, but to offer him a proper test that he could trust and enjoy. Until then, she decided, the best thing she could do was to keep learning.

A placebo, Ms Rao explained, is a dummy treatment, such as a sugar pill that has no medicine in it, and yet some people who take one do feel better, because their expectations have real effects on how they feel. This does not mean that they were imagining their pain, but it does mean that when a new medicine is tested, its results must be compared with those of a placebo. Otherwise we may give the credit to the treatment when it belongs to hope.

Ms Rao explained that the placebo effect is strongest for things that depend on how we feel, such as pain, tiredness and nausea. It does not mend a broken bone or cure an infection, which is why doctors measure real changes in the body as well as asking people how they feel. Even so, she said, the effect shows how closely the mind and the body are tied together.

Ms Rao poured the same orange juice into two cups, labelling one with a glossy sticker that promised the finest mountain oranges and the other with a plain scrawl that read juice. Almost everyone declared that the fancy cup tasted sweeter and fresher, even though both had come from the very same carton. What we expect, she said, shapes what we experience, and that is true for scientists as much as for anybody.

Ines drew two large circles on the whiteboard, one for the people who would receive the real treatment and another for those who would receive a dummy. Everything else about the two groups, from their age and their illness to the way they were looked after, had to be as alike as possible. If the real group improved more than the dummy group, only then could the treatment claim some credit.

To keep hopes from interfering, the best trials are blind, meaning that the volunteers do not know whether they have been given the real treatment or the dummy one. In a double-blind trial the researchers who hand out the treatments and measure the results are kept in the dark as well, so that neither the volunteers' expectations nor the scientists' own can quietly tilt the outcome. Only when the trial is over is the secret code finally opened and the truth revealed.

Around 1900 a horse in Germany, known as Clever Hans, became famous for apparently solving sums by tapping out the answer with his hoof. A careful investigator named Oskar Pfungst discovered that Hans failed whenever nobody in the room knew the answer, because he had been reading tiny, unconscious movements in the faces and bodies of his questioners. Nobody was cheating, and that is exactly why the experimenters' own knowledge had to be hidden.

In 1784 a French committee that included the American Benjamin Franklin investigated a fashionable healer who claimed to cure people with an invisible magnetic force. They blindfolded the patients and sometimes pretended to use the force when they were not, and the patients reacted to what they believed was happening rather than to what actually was. It was one of the first well-known blind tests, and it ended with a clear verdict.

Tomas boasted that he could always tell tap water from bottled water, so Amara poured eight pairs of cups marked only with secret codes that she had drawn by lot. With his eyes closed and nobody giving him hints, Tomas picked correctly in four of the eight pairs, which is exactly what guessing would produce. He laughed louder than anyone and said that the blind test had humbled him.

To make two fair groups, Ms Rao had the club draw names from a bag instead of letting people pick their own sides. If volunteers had chosen, she said, the keenest or the most hopeful might all have ended up together, and any difference between the groups would have been blamed on the treatment. Chance, used on purpose and with care, is the fairest referee that any experiment can have.

That evening Ines redrew her plan for testing the wristband, and this time it had every ingredient the club had learned. The bands would look identical, though only half of them would contain magnets, the groups would be chosen by lot, nobody would know who wore which, and everyone would score their backache from nought to ten each day. She closed the notebook with a feeling of excitement, knowing that she now had something fair to offer Mr Bello.

In the 1700s, scurvy was the terror of long sea voyages, and it killed far more sailors than enemy ships ever did. Men grew tired and pale, their gums swelled and bled, and wounds that had healed years before opened again. Nobody knew the cause, and every captain, doctor and sailor seemed to have a favourite remedy.

Some doctors recommended fresh air and exercise, others recommended vinegar, and others swore by a strong medicine made with acid. Every cure came with a few happy stories attached, but nobody had ever compared them side by side on sick men who were otherwise alike. It was exactly the kind of situation that Ines had learned to distrust, with plenty of confident opinion and very little fair evidence.

In 1747 a Scottish naval surgeon named James Lind was serving aboard a warship called the Salisbury, when scurvy began to spread among the crew. Rather than join the arguments about the cures, he decided to settle the matter with a trial, and he fitted it in among his daily duties. Lind was not yet famous, but he had a simple and very important idea about how to find out which cure really worked.

Lind picked twelve men who all had scurvy and whose symptoms were as similar as he could find, and he lodged them together in the same part of the ship. Every one of them ate the same basic diet, which meant that whatever he changed next would be the only difference between them. The reasoning was the same as the bean pots, Dev whispered, and Ms Rao nodded delightedly.

Lind divided the twelve men into six pairs and gave each pair a different daily remedy. One pair received cider, one pair vinegar and one pair sea water, while another pair swallowed a spicy paste, and yet another took drops of a strong acid medicine that doctors then admired. The last pair was given a daily ration of two oranges and one lemon, shared out carefully between them.

Dev jumped up and pointed at the chart of variables on the wall, because Lind had changed one thing, the remedy, while keeping the ship, the sailors' illness and their food the same. It was the bean experiment on a ship, he said, and Ms Rao beamed at him. A fair test, she said, does not depend on the century or on the size of the pots.

The results came quickly, and they were striking enough to catch the eye of anyone who studied the table. After about six days one of the two men who had eaten the oranges and lemons was fit to return to duty, and the other had recovered so well that he was given the job of nursing his sick shipmates. The other five pairs improved little, though the pair given cider seemed a little better than the rest.

Ms Rao reminded the club of what they had learned about chance, which was that twelve sailors in six pairs is a very small sample and could in principle have misled Lind. Even so, the design was so careful, and the effect of the fruit so much larger than the others, that the result was far more convincing than any single story. Later and larger tests, she added, would confirm that fresh fruit prevents and cures the illness.

Lind published his results in a book in 1753, yet the Royal Navy did not issue lemon juice to its sailors until the 1790s. Scientists identified the true cause of scurvy, a lack of vitamin C, only in the twentieth century, long after the fruit had been shown to work. Good evidence, it seems, does not always win quickly, and people sometimes need patience as well as proof.

Walking home, Dev peeled an orange and announced that twelve sailors and a notebook had done more good than a thousand opinions. Ines agreed, though she wondered what a scientist should do when a fair test is not possible, and when all we have are numbers that rise and fall together. It was a good question, and Ms Rao had promised to answer it on Thursday.

Ms Rao drew a graph showing that on days when more ice cream is sold, more people also have accidents in swimming pools and the sea. It would be absurd to conclude that ice cream causes accidents, she said, because a third factor, hot weather, makes people both buy ice cream and go swimming. Whenever two things go up and down together, a careful thinker therefore asks whether one causes the other, or whether something else is behind both.

Amara pulled out a chart from a school survey, which showed that children with bigger feet tended to score higher in reading tests. Nobody believed that large feet improve reading, because the hidden link was obvious once they thought about it: older children have bigger feet, and they have also had more years of practice. A pattern between two things, Ms Rao said, is a clue to be investigated, never a conclusion to be accepted.

A hidden third factor that leads to a false conclusion is called a confounder, Ms Rao said, and it is one of the most common traps in the study of cause and effect. People who carry lighters, for instance, are more likely to suffer from lung disease, not because lighters harm the lungs, but because people who smoke tend to carry them. Good experiments try to spot such factors and rule them out, by comparing groups that are otherwise alike.

Dev noticed that the captain of the school team scored more goals than anyone else, and he wondered whether wearing the armband made him play better. Ms Rao suggested that the arrow might point the other way, since coaches usually choose their best player to be captain, so the goals may have come first. When two things go together, she said, it is worth asking which came first and whether either caused the other.

A statistician once showed, as a joke with a serious point, that European countries with more nesting storks also have more babies born each year. Nobody should conclude that storks deliver the babies, because the answer is much more ordinary: bigger countries have more storks, and bigger countries have more people. The numbers were perfectly real, but the explanation that most people liked best, the one about delivery, turned out to be completely wrong.

Amara pasted two jagged lines onto the board that rose and fell in perfect step, even though they came from two unrelated lists of numbers. If you compare thousands of pairs of figures, Ms Rao explained, some of them are bound to match by pure chance, just as a lottery is bound to have a winner. A match that was found by hunting through everything, with no reason to expect it, deserves very little trust.

Whenever an experiment is possible, Ms Rao said, scientists assign people to groups by chance, just as the club had drawn names from a bag. Hidden factors such as age, weather, mood and diet then fall roughly equally into both groups, so a clear difference between them is far more likely to come from the treatment itself. It is the cleanest way that anyone has found to untangle a true cause from a mere coincidence.

Some questions cannot be answered with an experiment, because it would be wrong to ask people to start smoking just to see what happens. In the 1950s, British researchers followed tens of thousands of doctors for years instead, comparing those who smoked with those who did not, and the difference in lung disease was striking. When a fair experiment is impossible, Ms Rao said, scientists look for the next best evidence and are honest about its limits.

Ms Rao listed the signs that make us trust a claim about cause and effect, and the club copied them down. Many different studies by different teams point in the same direction, the cause comes before the effect, more of the cause produces more of the effect, and there is a believable explanation of how it works. No single sign is enough, she said, but together they build a strong case.

On the wall, beside the others, the club pinned a new rule in Amara's tidy lettering: linked does not mean caused. Whenever they heard that one thing was linked to another, they promised themselves to ask what else might connect the two, which came first, and whether it could be a coincidence. Dev added, in smaller letters at the bottom, that sometimes a link really is a cause, which is exactly why we must test.

Ms Rao drew a large bomber on the board and then marked it with red dots to show where the bombers returning from missions in the Second World War had been hit. The holes were mostly on the wings, the tail and the body, and she asked the club where the military should add heavy armour. It was a puzzle, she warned, and it had a trap hidden inside it that had caught many clever people.

Tomas said immediately that the armour should go wherever the holes were thickest, and the others nodded, because it sounded so sensible. Ms Rao asked a quiet question that stopped them: which planes were they actually looking at, and which planes were missing from the picture? The classroom went completely silent while twelve eyes studied the bomber and six brains tried to work out the trap.

The mathematician Abraham Wald, who worked with a group of statisticians in New York, saw the trick immediately. The bullet holes on the returning planes showed only the places where a plane could be hit and still make it home, because the planes that were hit elsewhere had never come back to be counted. The data, in other words, had been filtered by survival before anyone looked at it.

The conclusion was surprising, but it followed neatly: the armour belonged in the places where the returning planes had no holes at all, such as around the engines. A plane that was hit there was far less likely to return, so the missing holes were in a sense hidden in the missing planes. Ms Rao drew a bold blue circle around the engine, and Tomas groaned happily, because he had been so sure of his first answer.

Ms Rao admitted that this neat story is a simplified version, and that the real work had been much more laborious. Wald wrote page after page of difficult calculations to estimate how likely a plane was to survive a hit in each part of its body, and his methods were so careful that they are still studied today. Even good stories, she said, can be tidier than the truth, so it is wise to ask how we know.

Ms Rao wrote the words survivorship bias on the whiteboard in large letters and then underlined them twice for good measure. It happens whenever we study only the things that made it through some filter, such as the planes that returned, and forget the ones that did not, which may be quite different. The error is hard to notice, she said, precisely because the missing evidence is invisible.

Amara remarked that old buildings always seemed more beautiful and better made than new ones, and the others agreed. Ms Rao suggested that the poorly built and unloved old buildings had mostly been pulled down or had fallen over, so that what we see today is the best of their generation. The same trick applies to old songs, she added, since the forgettable ones were forgotten.

Dev interviewed his teammates on the field and found that every single one of them said that football was the best thing in the world. Ines pointed out gently that the children who had joined the team and then left were not standing there to be asked, and that their answers might have been very different. A survey that includes only the people who stayed, she said, tells you how happy the stayers are, not how good the club is.

Tomas brought a magazine in which a famous millionaire told how he had left school early and followed his dream to a fortune. Ms Rao asked about all the other people who had left school early, followed their dreams and ended up with nothing, and she pointed out that nobody writes magazine articles about them. Advice drawn only from the winners, she warned, can sound inspiring and still be quite misleading.

The club pinned a second card beside the first one, and it carried a question that Ines wrote in her best handwriting: who is missing from this picture? Dev said that it was the most annoying question in the world, and Ms Rao agreed that it was also one of the most useful. Whenever a claim looks too good, she said, look for the part of the story that nobody is telling.

Ms Rao told the club about a large hospital in Vienna in the year 1847, where thousands of mothers gave birth in two separate clinics. In those days nobody washed their hands carefully between patients, because the idea that tiny germs could pass illness from person to person had not yet been accepted. A dreadful fever, which took the lives of many new mothers, was a constant shadow over both clinics.

In the first clinic the mothers were looked after by doctors and medical students, while in the second clinic they were cared for by midwives. Strangely, far more mothers died of fever in the doctors' clinic, and the difference was so large that some frightened women pleaded to be admitted to the other one. Everyone agreed that something was badly wrong, but nobody could agree on what it was, and the fever kept returning.

A young Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis decided to find out why, and he tested one idea after another. The second clinic was in fact more crowded than the first, so crowding could not explain the deaths, and changing the position in which the mothers lay made no difference either. Each idea that failed the test was crossed off his list, which narrowed the search a little more.

Then, in 1847, Semmelweis's friend and colleague Jakob Kolletschka was cut by a student's scalpel while examining a dead body, and he soon died. Semmelweis studied the case and was struck by how much his friend's illness resembled the fever that was killing the mothers. A thought arrived like a flash of light: something from the dead body had got into the wound.

Semmelweis suddenly saw the difference between the two clinics, for the doctors and students often examined dead bodies in the morning and then went straight to examine the mothers, with unwashed hands. The midwives never worked with dead bodies at all, and their clinic had far fewer deaths. If he was right, he realised, the doctors themselves had been carrying the illness from bed to bed, without ever intending any harm.

Semmelweis turned his idea into a prediction that could be tested: if the doctors cleaned their hands thoroughly, fewer mothers would die. In May 1847 he ordered everyone who entered the ward to wash in a strong solution of chlorinated lime, a chemical that removes the smell of dead bodies. He did not know about germs, but he certainly knew how to design a test.

The effect was dramatic, and the numbers told the story more clearly than any speech could. Within a few months the deaths in the doctors' clinic had fallen sharply, until they were about as low as those in the midwives' clinic. Ines, looking at the graph that Ms Rao had drawn, felt a shiver at the thought of all the lives that a bowl of chlorinated water could save.

Despite his careful numbers, Semmelweis was met with indifference and even hostility by many doctors, some of whom were offended by the suggestion that they might have been spreading disease. The practice of washing hands was widely adopted only years later, when the work of other scientists on germs gave a clear explanation of why it worked. Good evidence, the story warns us, does not always win at once, because people are swayed by pride and habit, as well as by facts.

In the 1860s the work of Louis Pasteur on germs, and of the surgeon Joseph Lister on cleanliness in the operating room, finally explained why washing works. Semmelweis had died in 1865, before most doctors accepted his idea, and he never saw how completely the world would come to agree with him. Today, Ms Rao said, every doctor and nurse washes before touching a patient, and the habit saves lives every single day.

Before lunch the next day, Dev and Ines washed their hands at the school sink for a full twenty seconds, and they felt rather solemn about it. They talked about how Semmelweis had been right but had not persuaded people, and Ines wondered whether his message might have travelled further if it had been given more patiently. Being right is not enough, they agreed, because evidence also has to be explained clearly and kindly.

For many centuries, a large number of people believed that living creatures could simply appear from non-living things, a belief known as spontaneous generation. Maggots, they said, grew out of rotting meat, and mice arose from heaps of old rags and grain left in a dark corner. It was an easy thing to believe, since the maggots and mice really did turn up where the rubbish was.

In 1668 an Italian doctor named Francesco Redi tested the old belief by placing pieces of meat in several jars, leaving some open, sealing some tightly and covering others with fine cloth. Maggots appeared on the meat that flies could land on, but not on the meat that was sealed away, and on the cloth-covered jars they collected on the cloth. The idea that maggots came from nothing had been tested, and it had failed.

In the 1670s a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground tiny lenses of astonishing quality and used them to look at a drop of pond water. He saw a whole crowd of living things, far too small to see with the naked eye, and the old question returned with new force. Did these microbes come from other microbes, or did they spring up from the broth and water that they swam in?

In the 1860s Louis Pasteur faced critics who argued that sealed flasks proved nothing, because heating the broth and shutting out the air had spoiled the conditions for life. Pasteur accepted that this was a fair objection, and he set out to design a flask in which the broth could breathe fresh air but could not receive dust. Good scientists, Ms Rao said, turn the objections of their critics into better experiments.

In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur settled an old argument about whether tiny living things could arise from lifeless broth. He boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks that let air in but trapped dust and germs, and the liquid stayed clear for months, but when the neck was snapped off, it soon turned cloudy. The experiment gave a clean answer, and it is a model of how a clever design can answer a big question.

To be sure, Pasteur tilted one of his flasks so that the broth ran into the curved neck, where the dust had settled. Before long the liquid turned cloudy with growing microbes, which proved that the dust, and not the air itself, had carried them in. Every possible explanation was being tested in turn, and the unwanted ones were dropping out one by one.

Pasteur's chief opponent, a naturalist named Felix Pouchet, did not give up at once, and for a while the two men argued in public meetings and in print. The dispute was settled not by shouting but by more experiments, which other scientists could repeat and judge for themselves. In the end the evidence swung firmly behind Pasteur, and the idea that microbes arise from nothing faded.

The club decided to test where mould comes from, using three slices of bread: one left in an open dish, one sealed in a plastic bag, and one sealed in a bag with a damp cloth beside it. Ms Rao made everyone promise never to open the sealed bags, because mould spores can make some people sneeze or feel unwell. Amara wrote each prediction on a card and signed it, so that nobody could change their mind afterwards.

After a week, fuzzy patches of green and white mould had grown on all three slices, including the two that had been sealed in bags, and the damp bag had grown the most. Tomas was dismayed, until Ms Rao explained that the bread had not been heated like Pasteur's broth, so spores from the bakery and the kitchen were probably on it from the start. Their experiment was therefore weaker than Pasteur's, and the club wrote down exactly why.

Pasteur's discovery changed the everyday world, because once people knew that germs come from other germs, they could set about keeping them away. It led to pasteurised milk and wine, cleaner operating rooms and safer food, and it supplied the explanation that Semmelweis had lacked. Ines looked at the sealed bag of mouldy bread, thinking how a small, patient experiment can eventually protect millions of people.

Ms Rao asked a question that made the whole room go quiet: could the club measure the size of the entire Earth from the school field? The ancient Greeks, she told them, already had good reasons to believe that the Earth was round, such as the curved shadow it casts on the Moon during an eclipse and the way ships sink hull first beyond the horizon. Measuring its size, however, was a far bolder challenge, and it was first achieved by a librarian with a stick.

About 240 BC a Greek scholar named Eratosthenes worked as a librarian in the great library of Alexandria, in Egypt. In one of the scrolls he read that at noon on the longest day of summer, in the town of Syene far to the south, the Sun lit up the very bottom of a deep well. That meant the Sun was directly overhead there, and its rays were falling straight down.

On the same day in Alexandria, Eratosthenes pushed an upright stick into the ground and watched its shadow at noon. The stick still cast a short shadow, which meant that the Sun was not directly overhead there, even though it was straight overhead in Syene. Two places, the same Sun, the same moment, and yet two different results: something was bending the ground.

Ms Rao stood two sticks on a flat board and lit them with a torch held far away, and the two shadows came out exactly alike. When she stood the same sticks on different parts of a round ball, the shadows were different, and she explained that this was what Eratosthenes had seen. A flat Earth could not have produced two different shadows, so the surface had to be curved.

Eratosthenes measured the angle of the shadow and found that it was about one fiftieth of a full circle. The two towns, he had been told, were about 5,000 stadia apart, and so he reasoned that the whole way around the Earth must be fifty times as much. That gave him an answer of about 250,000 stadia, a figure reached with a stick, a well and a very clear head.

Nobody is certain how long a stadion was, because the Greeks used more than one length, and so historians still disagree about how accurate his answer was. If he used the shorter length, his figure was astonishingly close to the true distance around the Earth, which is about 40,000 kilometres, and if he used the longer one, he was too big by about a sixth. Either way, Ms Rao said, the method was brilliant, and she was careful not to claim more than we know.

Ms Rao telephoned her friend Mr Silva, who taught at a school in a town about 300 kilometres to the north, and asked whether his class would like to repeat the experiment of Eratosthenes. He agreed enthusiastically, and the two classes decided to measure the noon shadow of a one-metre stick on the same day. Tomas was put in charge of finding out exactly when noon was, which turned out to be harder than it sounds.

On the chosen day the club watched the shadow of a one-metre stick shrink as the morning went on, until at last it stopped shrinking and began to grow again. At that moment, which was the true local noon, Amara marked the tip of the shadow with chalk and Priya measured it with a tape. Three hundred kilometres to the north, Mr Silva's class was doing exactly the same thing, and their numbers arrived by message an hour later.

Amara and Priya drew the two shadows to scale on graph paper and worked out that the angles of the Sun in the two towns differed by about three degrees. A full circle has 360 degrees, so three degrees is one 120th of the way around, and the distance between the towns therefore had to be one 120th of the whole Earth. Multiplying 300 kilometres by 120, they arrived at 36,000 kilometres, and Tomas shouted that they had measured the world.

The atlas gave the distance around the Earth as about 40,000 kilometres, so the club's answer was roughly a tenth too small. Ms Rao said that this was a splendid result, since the blurry edge of a shadow and a slightly tilted stick can easily account for an error of that size. The club listed these sources of error in their notebooks, and with a stick, a tape measure and a telephone call, a group of children had measured the planet.

Ms Rao told the club a story about a prediction so risky that it might have destroyed the idea behind it. For more than two hundred years, Isaac Newton's theory of gravity had explained the fall of apples and the orbits of planets with astonishing success. In 1915, however, a physicist named Albert Einstein proposed a different theory of gravity, and it made a surprising claim.

Einstein's theory said that the Sun's gravity would bend the path of starlight passing close to it, so that stars near the Sun would appear to shift their positions slightly in the sky. The shift would be tiny, far smaller than anything the eye could see, but the new theory predicted twice as much bending as a simple version of the old one. Here at last was a clear difference that could be measured, and the measurement would decide between them.

There was a problem, however, because the stars that lie close to the Sun in the sky are lost in its glare and cannot be seen in ordinary daylight. Only during a total eclipse, when the Moon slides across the Sun and the sky darkens for a few minutes, do those stars become visible. The astronomers would have to wait for one, and then they would have to be in exactly the right place.

The plan was simple in outline and hard in practice: photograph the stars around the eclipsed Sun, then compare their positions with photographs of the same stars taken at night, when the Sun was somewhere else in the sky. If the stars seemed to have moved slightly outwards from the Sun, then its gravity had bent their light, and the amount of the shift would show which theory was closer to the truth. Everything depended on measuring extremely tiny distances on glass photographic plates, and on measuring them without a single careless slip.

A total eclipse was due on 29 May 1919, and its path crossed both Africa and South America, so two teams of astronomers set out with their telescopes. Arthur Eddington and a colleague went to the tiny island of Principe, off the coast of West Africa, while a second team sailed to the town of Sobral in Brazil. Two sites meant that if clouds ruined the view at one of them, the other might still save the whole expedition.

On the morning of the eclipse a heavy storm of rain swept over Principe, and Eddington feared that the long journey had been wasted. Shortly before the Moon covered the Sun the clouds began to thin, and the team worked through the minutes of darkness, changing plate after plate without stopping to look up. Only a few of their photographs showed enough stars to be useful, but a few was just enough.

Back home, the astronomers spent weeks measuring tiny distances on the glass plates, working in dim light with careful instruments. At Sobral the heat of the sun had slightly blurred the images of one telescope, so the team had to decide how far to trust that instrument, and they explained their choices in print so that others could judge them. Honest reporting of the awkward parts, Ms Rao pointed out, is part of the method.

In November 1919 the results were announced to a crowded meeting of scientists in London, and the news spread across the world within days. The starlight had bent by about the amount that Einstein predicted, and by clearly more than a simple version of Newton's theory allowed, so newspapers announced a revolution in science. There was some argument about the details, Ms Rao admitted, but much better measurements since then have agreed with the prediction.

The most important point, Ms Rao said, was that Einstein's theory had put its neck on the line, because the stars could easily have stayed exactly where they were. A risky prediction that survives a fair test is far stronger evidence than a safe one, and a theory that forbids a lot of possible results is saying a lot about the world. Dev suddenly realised that his own sock test had been the same kind of gamble.

Scientists, Ms Rao said, must be prepared to accept the verdict of a test, even when it concerns their own cherished idea and even when they would secretly prefer another answer. Ines wrote a new question in capital letters at the top of a clean page: what would show me that I am wrong? It was an uncomfortable question to ask about anything she believed, and she decided that this was precisely why it was the right one to ask next.

Dev, who enjoyed teasing, announced that there was an invisible cat in the science room that made no sound, left no hair and could not be touched. Ms Rao replied that this was not so much wrong as useless, because nothing that anyone could do would ever show it to be false, and a claim that can never be tested cannot be supported either. Scientists call an idea that could be contradicted by some possible observation falsifiable, and they value such ideas for exactly that reason.

Tomas sprinkled flour across the floor to catch paw prints, and Dev replied calmly that the cat floated and left none. Tomas hung a bell on a string where the cat might brush it, and then he sniffed hard for a smell, and each time Dev produced a fresh reason why the test could not work. The invisible cat, it seemed, had an excuse for everything, and Ines began to see that this was the whole problem.

Ms Rao explained that the invisible cat was not so much false as empty, because no result of any test could ever count against it. A useful idea, she said, forbids certain things: it says what we should not see, so that some observation could show it to be wrong, and this is what scientists mean by falsifiable. Ideas that forbid nothing explain nothing at all, however comforting or clever they may happen to sound.

For centuries, Europeans believed that all swans are white, which was a perfectly good idea because it could be tested, and every white swan they saw seemed to support it. In 1697 a Dutch explorer named Willem de Vlamingh saw black swans in Western Australia, and a single black swan was enough to show that the idea was wrong. A thousand white swans could never prove the claim, Ms Rao pointed out, but one black one could disprove it.

Tomas mentioned that his grandfather used a forked stick to find water underground, and that the old man swore it never failed. When it did fail, he explained that somebody in the group had been doubting, so that the stick could never be wrong, whatever happened. In careful tests, Ms Rao added, people who use such sticks usually do no better than guessing, and the excuse is a way of avoiding the test.

If a friend says that he saw a cat in the street this morning, you believe him without a second thought, because it is ordinary and costs you nothing to accept it. If he says that he saw the cat fly across the road, you would want a photograph, a second witness or at least a very good explanation, since the claim is so much larger. The bigger or stranger a claim is, the stronger the evidence we are right to ask for.

Ms Rao told the club that the responsibility for providing evidence rests with the person who makes a claim, and that it is not the duty of everyone else to disprove it. If a stranger announced that your school was built on a hidden underground lake, she said, nobody should have to dig up the playground to show that he was mistaken. This is often called the burden of proof, and it keeps discussions from becoming endless.

When the biscuits disappeared from the club's tin, Dev proposed that a ghost had taken them, whereas Ines pointed out the trail of crumbs that led to the dog's basket. It is usually wise to test the simplest explanation that fits all the facts before turning to something more elaborate, a habit known as Occam's razor. It is not a law of nature, of course, and sometimes the simple answer is wrong, but it is a good place to start.

By now the wall of the science room was covered with cards, and Ms Rao suggested that they gather them into a single toolkit of questions. What did we actually see, what else might explain it, which came first, what would show us wrong, and how strong is the evidence? Ines copied the list onto the inside cover of her notebook, where she knew she would see it every day.

Dev, who was never willing to lose a joke, suggested that perhaps the invisible cat was real and merely very shy. Ines laughed and agreed that it might be, but she pointed out that a creature that nobody could ever detect could not count as evidence for anything at all. The bell rang, the cat presumably stayed behind to guard the room, and the club went home still smiling.

Before trusting any claim that they came across online or in the news, the children learned to ask a short list of questions. Who is saying this, how could they possibly know it, what evidence do they offer, and would they gain money, fame or power if people believed them? The answers do not prove a claim true or false by themselves, but they show how much attention it deserves.

Ines followed the links on the webpage one by one, expecting each to lead her to a study, and each one led her instead to another page on the same site. At the end of the trail she found an online shop selling the miracle food, and not a single real experiment anywhere. The page, she realised, was not a report but an advertisement dressed up as a report.

On the way home, Dev pointed at a poster of a famous actor in a white coat, who claimed that a vitamin drink would make everyone stronger. Being brilliant at one job does not make a person an expert at another, Ines reminded him, and an actor in a white coat is still an actor. The right question was not who was famous, but who had actually studied the subject and tested the claim.

Ms Rao said that trusting experts is not laziness but a sensible way of living, since no one can test everything alone, and years of study do count for something. Even so, a good expert will explain the reasons behind a view, and a claim is more convincing when most researchers in the field reach the same conclusion by their own routes. When experts disagree, an honest account will say so openly, and a single lone voice, however confident, is rarely enough.

In 1912 a German scientist named Alfred Wegener suggested that the continents slowly drift across the surface of the Earth, and most experts of the day rejected the idea. It was not until the 1960s, when new evidence from the floor of the oceans appeared, that the scientific community changed its mind and accepted plate tectonics. A consensus of experts is strong evidence, Ms Rao said, but it earns its strength by being willing to change when the evidence does.

Before a study appears in most scientific journals, other experts in the field read the report, look for mistakes in the methods and ask awkward questions. This process, called peer review, catches a good many errors and weak arguments, although it is not perfect, and flawed studies sometimes slip through. Ms Rao described it as a quality check that is useful but not magical, and she urged the club to remember that publication alone is no proof.

In 2015, a large team of researchers set out to repeat one hundred published psychology experiments, and fewer than half of them produced the same clear result the second time around. The discovery alarmed many people, but it also showed science doing what it is meant to do, which is to examine itself, find weaknesses and improve its methods. Honest scientists do not claim to be perfect, and they trust the process because it is able to find and fix mistakes.

Ms Rao showed the club a headline announcing that a certain food doubles the risk of an illness, and asked them what it really meant. If the chance of getting the illness was one in a million and has now risen to two in a million, then the risk has indeed doubled, but it has barely changed in any way that matters to a life. Always look for the real numbers behind a relative change, and ask what the risk was to begin with.

Using exactly the same set of numbers, Ms Rao drew two graphs on the whiteboard, and they gave quite opposite impressions. On the first, the vertical axis began far above zero, so that a small rise looked like a leap, whereas on the second it began at zero and the same rise looked modest. Charts are not lies in themselves, but the club learned to read the labels and the scale before believing the shape.

To teach the club about cherry picking, Ms Rao asked Dev to describe the baskets of apples, and he proudly picked out only the fresh ones for his answer. Choosing just the examples that support a conclusion, while quietly ignoring the others, makes almost any claim look convincing, and it is a very common trick in advertising and arguments. A careful thinker therefore asks what has been left out, and tries to look at the whole of the evidence.

Dev remarked that the germ idea was only a theory, and Ms Rao smiled, because he had stumbled on a common confusion of words. In everyday speech, a theory often means a hunch, but in science it means a broad explanation that has been tested repeatedly and fits a large amount of evidence, as with the theory of gravity. A hypothesis is a tentative idea, whereas a theory has already survived many attempts to knock it down.

Ms Rao put three cards on the board, reading fact, law and theory, and she explained that they do different jobs. A fact is something we observe, a law describes a regular pattern in what we observe, and a theory is a broad explanation of why the pattern is there, so that a theory never graduates into a law. The fall of an apple is a fact, a law of gravity describes how strongly things pull on one another, and a theory of gravity tries to explain why they do.

A weather forecaster who announces a seventy per cent chance of rain is not being evasive, Ms Rao said, but is being exact about how much is known and how much is not. Scientists measure and report their uncertainty with ranges and margins of error, and these are signs of careful work and not of weakness. It is the person who claims to be absolutely certain about everything who should make us a little suspicious.

Amara learned to write her bean heights with a margin, such as 63 millimetres, give or take two. The margin told a reader how far the number could be trusted, and it reminded her that every measurement is an estimate rather than a perfect copy of the world. A result reported with its uncertainty, Ms Rao said, is more truthful, and therefore more useful, than one that pretends to be exact.

When Dev asked how many stars there were in the sky, Ms Rao admitted cheerfully that nobody knew the exact number, and that she did not know the answer to quite a few of his other questions, either. Saying that you do not know is not a failure but a starting point, because it opens the door to looking for evidence rather than inventing something to fill the gap. The best scientists are comfortable at the edge of their knowledge, and they say so.

Ines had always believed that going out in cold air gives you a cold, but when she looked it up she found that colds are caused by viruses. She crossed out her old note and wrote a new one beside it, adding that in winter we spend more time close together indoors, which gives the viruses more chances to spread. Changing her mind did not feel like losing, she realised, but more like a small step forward.

Ms Rao described the common warning signs of pseudoscience, which is something that looks like science without following its methods. They include vague claims that cannot be tested, a reliance on happy stories instead of data, a secret that no one is allowed to inspect, an attack on those who ask questions, and something expensive to sell. None of these signs proves that a claim is false, yet together they should make anyone check very carefully before they hand over their money.

Ms Rao handed out a pretend advertisement for a drink called Sparkle Tonic, which claimed to cure every illness known to humankind. The club ticked off the warning signs one by one: a secret recipe, a list of delighted customers, not a single test and a rather high price. Tomas wanted to know where he could buy a bottle, and everyone laughed, including Tomas.

The difference, Ms Rao explained, is not in the white coat or the long words, but in how the idea behaves when it is questioned. Real science invites tests, welcomes criticism and changes its mind when the evidence changes, whereas pseudoscience avoids tests, takes offence at criticism and protects its claims whatever happens. She added that people who are wrong about one thing may be right about others, so the club should judge claims rather than label the people who make them.

Dev found a dramatic photograph online, supposedly taken that very morning, and he was about to send it to everyone he knew. Ines suggested that they first search for the original source and the date, because pictures can be edited, taken from an earlier event or simply described with the wrong caption. A moment's checking before sharing is one of the most useful habits of the modern age, since false stories travel quickly.

Ms Rao observed that people are most easily fooled when a claim is something that they badly want to be true or badly fear, because strong feelings push aside careful thought. She told the club to treat a surge of excitement or anger as a signal to slow down and check the facts, instead of rushing to share or believe. Scientists are human too, so they build rules and checks into their work to protect themselves from their own wishes.

That evening a forwarded message arrived on Ines's phone, announcing that school would be closed the next day because of snow, and her heart leapt. She remembered Ms Rao's advice, took a long breath, and checked the school's own website instead of cheering, and there she found nothing at all about a closure. Nobody knew who had started the message, and she was glad that she had not passed it on to forty friends.

When Ines and Dev disagreed about how to read their results, the argument grew a little heated, until Ms Rao reminded them that the aim was to find out what was true, not to defeat each other. Ideas can be criticised sharply, but people deserve respect, and anybody, including a teacher, may be mistaken without being foolish. A scientific community works best when it is safe to say, I think that you have made an error, and when the reply is, let us look.

Looking back over the term, Ines noticed that nobody in the club had ever been laughed at for a wrong guess, not Tomas with his sand and his soil, not Dev with his socks and not herself with her beans. Ms Rao said that this was deliberate, because people who are afraid of being wrong hide their mistakes, and hidden mistakes are never corrected. A good club, like a good laboratory, is a place where it is safe to be wrong, and then to try again.

One clear evening, the two friends lay on the grass and looked up at the stars, and Ines said that she liked them even more now that she knew a little about them. Learning that the light left some of them thousands of years ago does not spoil the sight, she thought, but gives it depth and a sense of scale. Understanding how something works, as the club had learned, rarely takes away its wonder and usually adds to it.

For their final project, the club decided to ask whether listening to music helps people to remember a list of words. They planned two groups, one working in silence and one with music playing, and they chose who went where by drawing names from a bag, just as they had learned. Every pupil would study the same twenty words for the same two minutes, and Amara prepared the answer sheets in advance.

For their final project, the club asked whether listening to music helps people to remember a list of words, and they tested twenty classmates, ten in silence and ten with music playing. The silent group recalled slightly more words on average, but with so few people and so much natural variation, the difference was not large enough to be convincing. The honest conclusion, they decided, was that the result was unclear, and that they would need a larger sample and a repeat test to say more.

Ms Rao read Ines's plan for testing the wristband from top to bottom, and she said that it contained everything a fair test needs. Her one piece of advice was to offer it to Mr Bello as a friend and not as a judge, and to make it clear that the test was a way of finding out, and nobody was on trial. Ines nodded, put the plan in her bag and felt her heart beating a little faster.

Dev still pulled on his lucky socks before every match, because he enjoyed the ritual and it calmed his nerves, but he no longer pretended that they were affecting the score. He had learned that it is perfectly possible to enjoy a harmless habit while being honest about what it does, and about what it does not do. The only thing he refused to do any longer was to say that the socks had won the game.

At the end of the term Ines walked up to Mr Bello's garden gate with her notebook and kindly asked him the question that had started everything, namely how he could really know that his wristband worked. She was not trying to prove him wrong, but offering to help him design a fair test, and he was curious enough to agree. Thinking like a scientist, she had discovered, is less a matter of having the answers than of learning to ask how we would know.
